#9798. Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

#9797. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#9796. Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

#9794. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#9793. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

The idea of leasing out address space tied to a government block is fascinating, but the real worry is how much trust downstream networks place in who announces a prefix. One useful technical distinction is that AS2650 is an autonomous system, not a single subnet. For an observed exit IP, investigators still need the timestamp, the then-current BGP origin and prefix, RDAP allocation data, and corroborating telemetry; registration or geolocation alone does not identify the device or the proxy customer. That matters when a residential proxy makes traffic look trusted simply because the address falls inside an organization’s announced space. I maintain OnlinTools; our Subnet Calculator can show the network, range, broadcast address and host count for a supplied CIDR prefix, but it cannot establish route origin, physical location, ownership, or compromise.

Interesting how a seemingly ordinary device can turn a trusted network into an access point for someone else’s traffic.

What makes this particularly concerning is that the organization may remain completely unaware of how its own infrastructure is being used. A good reminder that information security also depends on visibility into what is actually happening within a network.

The location detail is what separates this from ordinary proxy noise: AS2650 is a fixed, well-known allocation, so any exit node registered there is either a misconfiguration worth escalating internally or an actual beacon worth watching – there’s no third reading. That Infatica nodes bundled into free apps are the vector fits the broader pattern where the resource being rented out belongs to someone who never knowingly agreed to rent it. The persistent two-week window suggests nobody at the network’s edge was watching egress, which is the cheap fix here.

#9792. AI Code Generation Is Only One Small Piece Of The ROI Equation

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

The short answer: To measure AI ROI in software engineering, look past how fast code gets written. Count the engineering hours your team spends after the code exists, on triage, diagnosis, prioritization, review, and release for escalated customer issues. Then estimate how much of that time AI could recover, and value it at a loaded engineering rate.

AI coding tools help engineers implement features and explore solutions faster. But faster code only gets teams partway to a positive return on AI. Teams still need to review, test, and release changes, then diagnose and resolve defects that reach customers.

That work depends on understanding how the code behaves in production, which customer configurations matter, and what previous failures revealed. When each team has to reconstruct the same production context, time saved in the editor gets spent again downstream.

A more complete way to measure AI ROI includes the effort required to verify, release, and support the software teams produce: the work of production engineering. Drawing on what we've seen with customers, we built an AI ROI calculator that estimates the capacity tied up in escalated customer work, and how much of it an engineering world model can recover by connecting the evidence teams need to cut redundant investigation and coordination. Together, they bring a broader opportunity into focus: preserving more of the gains from faster coding and making each resolution useful beyond the issue that prompted it.

Run the AI ROI calculator to estimate how much engineering capacity your team could recover.

Faster implementation gives teams room to test ideas, refine features, and respond to customers. Those gains become harder to realize when the surrounding workflow still depends on people rebuilding the same explanation.

DORA's 2026 report, The ROI of AI-assisted Software Development, emphasizes that faster coding doesn't automatically translate into business value. It identifies reducing unnecessary rework as a way to reclaim engineering capacity and increase output without expanding headcount.

For teams already investing in AI code generation, that opens another investment question: how much capacity could AI recover from the work triggered by production defects? Customer escalations still require investigation, fixes need prioritization, and corrective changes need verification before release. Those responsibilities create an opportunity to extend AI's value beyond producing code.

An escalated customer issue makes those dependencies visible. Support rebuilds the customer's history. Engineering traces the failure through code and runtime evidence. Product seeks a reliable account of its impact, while QA establishes the conditions the fix needs to satisfy. When those findings stay scattered across tickets and conversations, each handoff adds another round of explanation.

Much of this effort is easy to miss because it appears inside otherwise necessary work. Investigating a defect is necessary; reconstructing evidence that another team has already assembled adds avoidable effort. Reviewing a change is necessary; asking its author to recover the reasoning behind its scope adds more.

The loss extends beyond labor cost: slower resolutions, interrupted feature work, less time for prevention, and senior engineers diverted into repeated explanations. Recovering that capacity means addressing repeated work across the full production workflow, from the first customer report to a verified release.

PlayerZero's engineering world model connects code, production signals, customer tickets, and prior outcomes into a persistent context that teams and agents share. Support, engineering, product, and QA can work from the same evidence about how the system behaves and what previous investigations established.

Shared context helps work move between teams without losing intent or scope. A discovery in support becomes available to the people and agents responsible for diagnosis, prioritization, and validation, reducing the work each team repeats.

PlayerZero's AI ROI calculator puts a number on that question for teams already using AI coding tools. It estimates a practical portion of the opportunity: recoverable effort across escalated customer work and the cost equivalent of that capacity.

Assembling evidence and coordinating escalations

Less escalation overhead and fewer clarification requests

Reconstructing symptoms and prior investigative work

More engineering capacity for unresolved causes

Establishing customer impact, related requests, and priority

Faster, better-informed decisions about engineering work

Reacquiring the fix context and rebuilding validation scenarios

Less review rework, and more focused release validation

The calculator uses illustrative effort assumptions and a loaded engineering rate to estimate the capacity teams could redirect toward planned delivery and reliability. The cost equivalent values that time before platform costs, providing a starting point for weighing the investment. The four stages below illustrate the repeated work reflected in the estimate and where shared context can reduce it.

Support's contribution begins well before a backend engineer picks up a ticket. L1 support clarifies the report and responds to the customer; support engineers connect it to sessions, documentation, related tickets, and technical evidence.

When those sources are disconnected, preparing an escalation becomes an investigation in its own right. Customer follow-up stretches out while support coordinates the people who might have the answer.

Consider a hypothetical customer whose data export times out when they request a large dataset with a particular filter enabled. Smaller exports still succeed. A report that simply says "exports are broken" leaves engineering with substantial work to do before it can investigate the cause.

PlayerZero connects customer reports to the relevant code and runtime conditions. In this example, support can pass along the affected configuration, request traces, and findings about which exports succeed or fail. The engineering world model keeps those findings connected to the report, giving engineering a defined technical case and support evidence for customer updates.

The immediate gain is less effort to prepare and clarify the escalation. Across a busy support queue, this returns time to customer work and reduces the interruptions needed to make an engineering ticket actionable. That means support can keep customers informed without every update depending on a specialist engineer's availability.

Backend engineers contribute specialized judgment, but a fragmented escalation can consume their time before they reach the unresolved question. They inspect logs and traces, review code history, and test competing explanations. If support's findings or a previous investigation are missing, they also retrace work that the organization has already completed.

That effort interrupts feature development and concentrates investigations around engineers who remember the affected system. The cost includes both the investigation and the planned work waiting for those engineers to return.

For the export timeout scenario, agentic debugging uses connected runtime evidence and code history to point to a query changed in a recent release. The engineering world model incorporates support's findings into this investigation, alongside the relevant changes, failure conditions, and explanations already considered. The engineer then checks that hypothesis against current behavior and determines whether the query accounts for the timeout.

Once confirmed, the cause and supporting reasoning become part of the same context, alongside support's original findings. Ruled-out explanations remain available, too, so another engineer can understand why the investigation settled on that path. Resolving escalations places fewer demands on the specialist engineers who know the system best, preserving their capacity for planned development. Their judgment goes toward evaluating the cause and choosing a correction rather than recovering the history behind it.

A confirmed cause gives product managers and engineering leads a technical basis for prioritization. They still need to connect customer impact to technical scope before deciding what takes precedence over planned work.

When that evidence is disconnected, effort accumulates in reconciling related requests, agreeing on the immediate response, and explaining why it matters more than competing priorities.

The engineering world model keeps related customer reports connected to the internal engineering issue, so product can assess customer impact alongside the diagnosis and proposed correction. In the export example, the team can distinguish an urgent query fix from a broader request to redesign exports, then connect that scope decision and its rationale to the technical findings and affected customer workflows.

Engineering begins implementation with both the technical findings and the reason for the chosen response. Carrying agreed priorities and scope into the work reduces coordination demands and the need for repeated scope discussions, helping the team protect planned delivery.

A prioritized fix still needs implementation, review, testing, and release. Backend engineers implement the correction, while reviewers and QA determine whether it resolves the failure without disrupting working behavior. Reconstructing the intended outcome, affected configurations, and regression coverage delays release decisions and consumes capacity that could otherwise go toward evaluating the change itself.

Coding assistance can accelerate the query change in the export example. The engineering world model carries the diagnosis and agreed scope into validation: the large, filtered export should complete successfully and return the expected records, while previously successful exports continue to work.

Those conditions guide review, code simulations, and regression testing. Simulations predict behavior without executing the code, helping the team focus tests on potential risks; testing establishes whether the change meets the intended outcome.

With less effort spent reconstructing validation requirements, reviewers and QA can concentrate on correctness and relevant coverage. Release decisions are better informed, with engineering time going toward verifying the fix rather than recovering why it was needed.

After release, the engineering world model keeps validation results and production observations connected to the original report, diagnosis, and scope decision. Support and SRE teams can see what the fix covered, whether the customer's export succeeded, and what remains unresolved. That completed record gives support a grounded closing explanation and preserves the evidence behind the resolution.

The engineering world model's value extends beyond the effort saved on the current issue. PlayerZero's shared organizational memory makes configuration findings, decisions, and their rationale available across teams, so lessons from one investigation can inform future work.

PlayerZero's approach to memory and learning captures useful findings from completed work and incorporates corrections as conditions change, keeping the organization's accumulated experience useful over time. Teams can build on those findings while checking them against current evidence, rather than reconstructing each investigation from scratch.

One customer's experience shows how shared production understanding can extend across functions. At Higher Logic, a PlayerZero pilot on its Vanilla product line gave support visibility into the code behind customer reports, helping the team investigate and resolve eligible defects within engineering-defined boundaries. Support shipped fixes for 50 customer issues in two months. The company also reports 250 engineering hours reclaimed from support escalations.

QA adoption emerged from support's use of the platform. The QA team used the same visibility into code-change impact to identify areas likely to be affected by a release and prioritize testing. The production understanding that helped support resolve customer work gained another application in release quality, extending its usefulness across the organization.

Shared knowledge also affects the operating cost of AI work. Workflow memory carries lessons between runs, while concise handoffs carry completed work and decisions between stages. Retained findings and concise handoffs reduce repeated retrieval and reasoning, lowering the operating waste involved in reaching a useful outcome.

The calculator estimates recoverable effort in escalated work. The broader return comes as the same learning improves support, engineering, product, and QA work over time, including opportunities to prevent a known failure from becoming another customer escalation.

Use the AI ROI calculator to estimate the capacity your team could recover from escalation volume, resolution effort, and loaded engineering cost. Put that estimate alongside the longer-term value of shared learning: fewer repeated investigations, more focused validation, and more engineering time for the product and reliability improvements your customers need.

Start with the time AI coding assistants like GitHub Copilot save during implementation. Then account for what happens after the code exists: review, testing, triage, and defect resolution. Value the net hours your team recovers at a loaded engineering rate and compare that against tool and platform costs. Coding speed on its own overstates the return.

Code generation speeds up one stage of delivery. If review, testing, triage, and diagnosis still depend on people rebuilding the same production context, the time saved in the editor gets spent again downstream. DORA's research makes a similar point: the biggest returns come from reducing unnecessary rework, not from writing code faster.

It should measure capacity across the full production workflow, not just coding output. PlayerZero's AI ROI calculator estimates recoverable effort in escalated customer work across four stages: support and triage, engineering diagnosis, product intake, and build, verify, and release. It values that time at a loaded engineering rate, before platform costs.

DORA describes AI adoption as a J-curve: teams often see a temporary dip while they learn the tools and adjust workflows, before longer-term returns show up. Escalation work is a good place to look early because the effort is easy to count. At Higher Logic, support shipped fixes for 50 customer issues within two months of its PlayerZero pilot.

DORA's framework models the financial return of AI-assisted development across software delivery as a whole. PlayerZero's AI ROI calculator focuses on one place that return leaks: the effort escalated customer issues pull from support, engineering, product, and QA. Used together, they show both the overall picture and a specific, recoverable source of capacity.

#9791. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

What will you build? Share your scene and results in the Hugging Face comments, including the assets and Isaac Sim version you used.

So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

#9789. Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities

Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

#9788. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9787. Human in the Loop AI: How to Safely Scale Agentic Workloads with Tunable Autonomy

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Human-in-the-loop AI keeps people in charge of key decisions, while tunable autonomy lets teams expand what AI agents handle on their own as trust grows.

Most organizations experimenting with agentic AI run into two barriers long before they reach meaningful automation: the trust gap and the accountability gap. While teams trust AI enough to summarize tickets and recommend fixes, they don't yet trust it to investigate incidents or implement code changes on its own. And even when AI performs well, this doesn't transfer responsibility. Someone still needs to own the decision and be ready to reverse it if it goes sideways.

In mature engineering environments, both concerns are justified. Large codebases, shared infrastructure, customer commitments, and compliance requirements make it risky to let AI move from recommendation to autonomous action without oversight.

That’s why the answer is not full autonomy or full human control—it’s tunable autonomy that you can adjust as you progress in your AI adoption. With this operating model, organizations progressively expand what AI can do as trust grows, all while keeping a clear human owner at critical stages and full control over automated workflows.

Most teams begin with simple AI workflows, like summarizing incidents, explaining code changes, and drafting pull requests. The results are fast, and the downside is low—if the summary is wrong, a human catches it before anything breaks.

Those early wins create pressure to automate more. Leaders begin asking whether AI can take on higher-stakes work, such as classifying incidents, preparing fixes, and closing tickets.

That is where adoption stalls. That's why human-in-the-loop design matters.

Not all AI decisions carry the same weight. The same AI action that’s safe in one workflow can be dangerous in another. Auto-closing a duplicate support ticket carries almost no risk. Auto-deploying a production fix carries enormous risk. The action looks similar, but the consequences aren't.

And a single bad action is recoverable. What's harder to reverse is an agent that executes multiple steps on the same incorrect assumption. Consider an agent that prepares the wrong remediation plan. From there, it validates the wrong outcome and closes the wrong ticket. A small mistake turns into a cascading failure that grows harder to reverse.

The solution isn't to abandon AI altogether. The real leverage comes from building deliberate stopping points into the workflow. These checkpoints create a moment for human review before a mistake propagates, and establish a clear owner for the work that crosses that threshold. Over time, those approvals become the evidence base for every decision that advances AI's role.

The question, then, becomes how to place these checkpoints deliberately—and how to know when you have earned enough trust to remove one.

That is the problem tunable autonomy is designed to solve.

Tunable autonomy gives teams explicit control over how much AI agents can do at each stage of a specific workflow. Rather than making a one-time choice between full human control and full autonomy, organizations can set autonomy levels tailored to each workflow stage.

For each stage, they choose from the four levels:

The following table shows where most organizations start, and where each stage can realistically go.

Different workflows should progress at different speeds, and organizations should tune autonomy by repository, service, severity, ticket type, or team.

Setting AI autonomy levels within a team is relatively straightforward. Things get much more complicated when work crosses a team boundary. That's where introducing AI autonomy gates—checkpoints that determine whether AI-driven work can advance to the next stage or domain—matters most.

The reason is simple—each team has different standards, conventions, risk tolerances, and implicit knowledge, so they see the same issue differently. Support sees customer impact, engineering sees code paths, and QA sees reproduction risk.

Say an AI agent is classifying incoming support tickets. The agent’s actions stay within a single team’s domain, so the risk of a misstep is low and contained. When approval rates for AI-driven classifications trend near 100%, that workflow becomes a strong candidate for autonomous operation within your defined guardrails.

Now, say an AI-assisted workflow crosses a team boundary, like an AI-diagnosed issue moving from support to engineering with a recommended fix attached. The stakes rise because the fix comes with root-cause assumptions baked in—if one is wrong, it can travel through diagnosis, remediation, and closure before anyone with the right context catches it. And since engineering has to act on work they didn't produce, accountability for the outcomes becomes ambiguous.

That's exactly where an autonomy gate belongs. The gate ensures the work has been reviewed by someone who can vouch for it before it crosses that line. Each successful handoff, reviewed and acted on without issue, is how AI earns the next level of trust to take on more work.

To implement the tunable autonomy model across your organization, start by establishing full human-in-the-loop approval at every critical stage.

Even in recommend-only mode, AI creates immediate value for engineering teams. Connecting tickets to code, telemetry, and runtime behavior compresses investigation time to minutes. Surfacing likely root causes and recommending fixes streamlines resolutions, increasing customer satisfaction. Drafting pull requests and incident summaries keeps engineers focused on building.

Your team stays in the loop at every step, reviewing and course-correcting before anything moves forward. When their approvals reach close to 100% across workflows, gradually increase autonomy based on the following factors.

When you’re scaling AI workflows, you’re not just asking “Can the AI do this task?” but “Can it do it reliably enough to justify less oversight?” Metrics provide the most objective answer to this question.

Most engineering organizations already track these metrics for delivery performance and incident management. What changes with AI is what they reveal. Each one now also measures a different dimension of AI’s reliability.

Think of it less like flipping a switch and more like a new hire earning the right to make decisions without running them by a manager. Nobody hands over full autonomy on day one. It's granted incrementally by demonstrating sound judgment, catching mistakes before they compound, and building a track record that speaks for itself.

Autonomy can't advance without the professional judgment to back it. Approval from experienced team members ensures AI systems perform well across both familiar conditions and edge cases that only emerge under pressure.

Teams that get autonomy expansion right exercise their judgment across the dimensions where AI has the most influence and the least visibility: people, process, and context. They follow the same three questions before extending AI’s responsibilities further.

While metrics show that trust is building, satisfying these criteria tells you whether it's actually earned. When AI understands enough about your systems, your people, and your processes, it changes how work flows across the organization, increasing resilience and shifting defect resolution from reactive to proactive.

A helpful mental model is to apply the same bar you’d use for a senior engineer. Instead of micromanaging them, you trust that they've internalized the business context, know how handoffs work, and can navigate team processes without a checklist. An AI agent has to earn that same confidence, and teams need to build the evidence that it has.

Key Data’s experience is a blueprint for what it looks like when people, process, and context align with the metrics. By connecting customer-reported issues to the exact code changes and runtime behavior behind them, they eliminated the ambiguity that makes teams hesitant to rely on AI. With that context and the ability to reproduce and diagnose problems in minutes instead of weeks, the confidence to go further with AI across their workflow followed naturally.

Safe autonomy depends on strong controls—not just as a brake on what AI can do, but as the foundation that makes expanding its responsibilities possible. Despite differences in scale, stack, and risk tolerance, what those controls actually require tends to look the same across organizations.

The most trustworthy AI systems converge on four properties.

While these properties create a foundational audit system that keeps autonomy from becoming a liability, they're not sufficient on their own. Certain actions carry significant organizational weight, making human review essential regardless of how well the AI has been performing.

In these situations, the cost of getting autonomy wrong outweighs the efficiency gains from skipping the review. That’s why a checkpoint there almost always pays for itself.

The point isn’t to eliminate risk—it’s to make it manageable. AI agents will make mistakes, but they’ll make fewer than their human counterparts. With those controls in place, you can scale or decrease autonomy across teams while keeping errors contained and accountability clear.

At Cyrano Video, the combination of richer context and stronger trust allowed support teams to resolve more issues independently. As a result, the company reduced engineering time spent on support and bug fixes by roughly 80% while preventing many tickets from escalating in the first place.

Tunable autonomy only works when AI has access to the full engineering context—but in most organizations, that context is scattered across systems that don't talk to each other, leaving AI to act on an incomplete picture.

PlayerZero creates that visibility by unifying these signals into an engineering world model: a single representation of the system that connects intent, impact, real-world behavior, and institutional knowledge.

That foundation gives AI agents everything they need to meet the three conditions that teams use to validate readiness for higher autonomy: deep business understanding, clear visibility into ownership and escalation paths, and a reliable picture of process execution.

Cayuse shows what this model unlocks in practice. Using PlayerZero, they gave teams earlier visibility into issues and stronger confidence in the accuracy of AI-driven investigations. As a result, they found and fixed 90% of issues before users noticed and cut average resolution time by 80%.

Most organizations treat autonomy as a destination. The ones that scale it successfully treat it as a practice—something earned through evidence, refined through metrics, and extended only when trust is real.

That shift in mindset is what separates teams that adopt agentic AI from teams that build a lasting advantage with it.

PlayerZero is built for organizations that want to move fast with AI—without outrunning their ability to control it—giving teams the foundation to extend autonomy safely and the evidence to know when to go further. Book a demo to learn how.
