#9772. 5 Banking Compliance Risks Every Independent Contractor Needs to Understand

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Suppose you just closed the best quarter of your independent career. You signed three new international clients, doubled your monthly billings, set aside your quarterly tax estimate, and finally have enough surplus cash to move a healthy chunk into your brokerage account. From where you sit, you are the exact kind of upwardly mobile customer any financial institution should roll out the red carpet to keep.

Inside the bank’s automated risk engine, that exact same month looks like a four-alarm fire. After 25 years working inside traditional retail and commercial banking, I have sat in the compliance review meetings where accounts like yours land on the chopping block. When the bank’s Transaction Monitoring System (TMS) scans your ledger at two in the morning, it does not see your GitHub commits, your pitch decks, or the late-night Zoom calls behind your invoices. It sees a sudden spike in cross-border velocity, wires arriving from three unrelated corporate entities in different jurisdictions, and rapid outbound transfers to external investment or fintech platforms. In compliance shorthand, your breakout quarter reads like textbook layering or unlicensed commercial activity running through a retail checking account.

Traditional consumer banking infrastructure was built for a 20th-century economic citizen. The entire retail model assumes one local employer, one predictable domestic payroll deposit hitting on the 1st and the 15th of every month, and predictable local debit card spending on groceries, utilities, and a domestic mortgage. Today, millions of legitimate software engineers, independent consultants, indie founders, and remote contractors earn clean global income, yet their banks routinely freeze their balances, hold incoming wires in review queues, demand invasive documentation, or reject their mortgage applications outright.

Banks do not punish self-employed people and remote workers out of personal malice. They punish them because of brutal compliance unit economics and rigid statistical risk modeling. Once you understand how those internal calculators work, you can stop taking account reviews personally and start structuring your finances to reduce avoidable false positives and survive routine compliance checks intact.

A standalone personal checking account is frequently a money-loser for a commercial bank unless you carry a substantial, idle cash balance or borrow money at high interest rates. Banks earn retail margins on the net interest spread (taking your low-cost deposits and lending them out) and on interchange fees when you swipe your card. According to StrategyCorps’ retail checking performance benchmarks, roughly 40 percent of all retail checking relationships are unprofitable for the institution holding them. In its analysis of nearly four million consumer checking relationships drawing on research from groups including the American Bankers Association (ABA) and the FDIC, StrategyCorps notes that maintaining and servicing a checking account costs a bank an estimated USD 250 to USD 400 per year, meaning accounts generating less than USD 350 in annual fee and net interest revenue fail to cover their baseline operating overhead. When a remote worker receives a large payment and immediately sweeps most of it into an external treasury bill account, a multi-currency fintech app, or an index fund, the bank absorbs all the regulatory liability of clearing the payment without keeping the deposit long enough to earn meaningful net interest income on it.

Meanwhile, missing a single bad actor can be catastrophic. Look at what happened when FinCEN assessed a record USD 1.3 billion penalty against TD Bank after regulators found that its monitoring systems failed to catch illicit peer-to-peer transfers and funnel account activity. Across the industry, compliance departments operate in a state of permanent defensive paranoia. According to a 2024 LexisNexis Risk Solutions study conducted by Forrester Consulting, financial crime compliance costs across the United States and Canada have reached USD 61 billion per year, with 99 percent of institutions reporting rising expenses and over 80 percent facing growing screening alert volumes.

To protect themselves from nine-figure regulatory fines, banks tune their automated monitoring rules to be hyper-sensitive. Those hair-trigger rules generate a mountain of false positives on ordinary people doing ordinary work, a friction point that even the FFIEC’s suspicious activity examination manual openly acknowledges. According to McKinsey’s research on financial crime operations, more than 90 percent of transaction-monitoring alerts at most banks turn out to be false positives, and banks report that as much as 85 percent of their anti-money laundering (AML) and financial crime activities remain manual, administrative, or nonanalytical, such as pulling data out of one internal system to key it into another. An empirical study of 19 major U.S. banks by the Bank Policy Institute illustrated the sheer scale of that funnel: participating institutions employed more than 14,000 compliance workers and reviewed roughly 16 million alerts in a single year to file 640,000 Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs), with law enforcement following up on a median of just 4 percent of those filed reports. By Fiscal Year 2025, as documented in the FinCEN Year in Review, nationwide SAR filings climbed to roughly 4.8 million for the year, including 2.8 million reports filed by depository banks and another 1.26 million filed by money services businesses.

Here is the internal banking math that nobody explains to you at account opening. Every time an automated rule flags your incoming wire, a Level 1 compliance analyst has to open a ticket, pull your customer file, inspect your ledger, and decide whether to clear the alert or escalate it to a Level 2 investigator. Having a trained human read a foreign consulting contract, check a corporate registry in Estonia or Singapore, chase down customer documents, and write a formal audit memo justifying why a SAR was not filed consumes expensive specialist labor. Both the Wolfsberg Group’s statement on effective suspicious activity monitoring and FinCEN’s October 2025 interagency SAR FAQs have explicitly warned that over-alerting and defensive compliance routines drain real institutional resources on low-value noise.

When a low-fee checking account already sits near or below the bank’s USD 250 to USD 400 annual servicing break-even line, repeated manual compliance reviews and cross-border document checks quickly push that relationship deep into the red. Once a customer’s incremental compliance cost outweighs whatever modest deposit margin they bring in, banks do not hire extra analysts to study your freelance career. They simply "de-risk" you by restricting the account, mailing you a cashier’s check for your remaining balance, and terminating the relationship.

Regulators know this is happening, and they have called banks out on it repeatedly. In the United States, the Treasury Department’s 2023 strategy report on financial-sector de-risking confirmed that customer profitability, weighed directly against available compliance resources and AML system costs, is the primary driver behind institutions cutting off entire categories of customers. Across the Atlantic, the European Banking Authority’s guidelines on unwarranted de-risking and the global FATF policy statement on the risk-based approach both warn that wholesale offboarding of customer groups is a sign of ineffective risk management rather than sound compliance. Still, until regulators penalize banks as heavily for closing legitimate accounts as they do for missing money launderers, the unit economics inside your bank will not change.

Automated Transaction Monitoring Systems do not evaluate your character; they measure statistical deviation against predetermined rulesets. When independent professionals get locked out of their accounts, the review can almost always be traced back to one (or an ugly combination) of five mechanical triggers.

The most common self-inflicted wound I see among independent earners is what I call the Ghost Student Problem. Think back to when you actually opened your primary checking account. For many professionals in their late twenties or thirties, that account was opened eight or ten years ago when they were university students or entry-level local employees. During onboarding, you answered a quick questionnaire estimating your monthly deposit volume at USD 2,000 with zero international wire activity.

Fast-forward to today, and you are pushing USD 12,000 a month in cross-border software engineering or advisory retainers through that exact same account without ever updating your customer file. Under the FFIEC’s Customer Due Diligence examination rules, banks are required to build a customer risk profile at onboarding and use expected transaction types and volumes as the baseline for detecting suspicious activity. Those same examination standards identify unexplained changes in account activity and shifts in employment or business operations as direct triggers for event-driven risk reviews. The bank’s algorithm is not comparing your current income against the reality of your senior career. It is comparing a USD 12,000 international inflow against the stored baseline of a 20-year-old college student, flagging an immediate anomaly for activity inconsistent with the customer profile.

When you operate as a solo consultant or a one-person digital business, it is easy to view your revenue as your personal paycheck. To a bank’s risk engine, however, a salaried employee receiving domestic payroll and an independent contractor collecting client invoices belong in two completely different regulatory universes. Banks run separate monitoring models for retail consumers and commercial entities because business accounts naturally involve multiple counterparties, higher payment velocity, and international invoicing.

When you route Stripe payouts, platform settlements, or direct corporate wires into a standard personal checking account, you are feeding commercial transaction patterns into a consumer risk model. Worse, you are almost certainly violating the contract you signed when you opened the account. Traditional institutions like Associated Bank explicitly prohibit business activity in personal deposit agreements, and modern fintech platforms enforce the exact same boundary, as seen in Wise’s official rules separating personal and business accounts. Giving a bank a clear Terms of Service violation is the fastest way to get offboarded without appeal, because the institution does not even need to suspect illicit activity to close an account used in breach of its deposit contract.

Suppose a client pays you USD 5,000 on Tuesday morning into your primary bank or a multi-currency fintech app like Wise or Revolut. Because you manage your money actively, you log in two hours later and transfer USD 4,500 out to a brokerage account, a high-yield savings account at another institution, or a regulated crypto exchange. To a financially literate human, moving idle cash into higher-yielding assets immediately is smart personal treasury management.

To an anti-money laundering algorithm, near-zero balance retention paired with rapid inbound-to-outbound turnover closely mirrors the behavioral signature of a transit or funnel account. If you read the FFIEC’s official list of money-laundering red flags, one of the classic funds-transfer indicators is incoming deposits or transfers being received and "almost immediately, all or most of the transfers or deposits" being wired onward in a manner inconsistent with the customer’s history. Similarly, FinCEN’s advisory on funnel accounts highlights rapid withdrawals occurring with little time elapsing after deposits, while the FBI’s guidance on money mule networks explains how criminal syndicates use unwitting or complicit intermediaries to receive and forward funds to add layers of distance. Although FFIEC guidance notes that a single red flag is not proof of crime on its own, treating your checking account like a revolving door where money never rests overnight routinely trips pass-through velocity rules.

Modern remote work relies on a patchwork of global payment rails, and those rails often mangle the data your receiving bank needs to see. You might have one client paying you via SWIFT from London, another sending EUR via SEPA from Berlin, a third routing your retainer through a global payroll aggregator like Deel or Payoneer, and a fourth paying you in USDC or USDT stablecoins that you off-ramp into fiat through a licensed exchange.

Here is what happens under the hood when payments pass through intermediaries and payroll platforms. Instead of sending a direct wire from your client’s corporate bank account, many payment processors batch their payouts and disburse funds through local pooled accounts or net settlement rails. As detailed in the Wolfsberg Group’s 2026 guidance on banking non-bank payment service providers, bundled transactions and high levels of intermediation between the original payer and final beneficiary make it significantly harder for banks to screen counterparties and verify the underlying commercial flow. By the time an intermediated ACH or SEPA credit hits your bank, the original client’s name is often replaced in the header by a third-party payment processor or settlement bank, matching another FFIEC Appendix F red flag covering large third-party processor ACH credits from originators the receiving bank has never vetted. If you cash out stablecoin payroll from an exchange, the bank sees fiat arriving from a virtual asset platform, a flow that both FinCEN’s advisory on convertible virtual currencies and the FATF’s virtual asset red-flag report subject to heightened source-of-funds scrutiny whenever the bank lacks clear visibility into the underlying business activity.

Remote workers love the freedom to work from anywhere, but banking security engines are deeply territorial. When you log into your domestic banking app from a cafe Wi-Fi network in Bali, Lisbon, or Belgrade, or when you open your banking portal while connected to a commercial VPN node in another country, you trip a separate layer of defense: the fraud, e-banking, and sanctions screening engine.

As outlined in the FFIEC’s Electronic Banking examination overview, banks treat online banking outside their targeted geographic footprint as a heightened risk factor and actively monitor Internet Protocol (IP) address reports alongside funds-transfer velocity to spot account anomalies. Cybersecurity engines also track device fingerprints and network routing to stop account takeovers and enforce geographic sanctions. If your account logs in from Chicago on Monday morning and appears to log in from a shared VPN address in Southeast Asia or Eastern Europe four hours later, the system flags an "impossible travel" event or a high-risk jurisdiction login. Even when the lock starts as an automated fraud or sanctions precaution, unfreezing the account often triggers a manual back-office review of your recent ledger, turning a routine travel lock into a broader AML inquiry.

Nothing infuriates a legitimate freelancer more than the wall of silence that follows an account freeze. You call customer support in a panic because your rent is due, and the representative reads from a wooden script: "Your account is currently under review by a back-office team, and we cannot provide any further details or a timeline." When they eventually close the account, the termination letter usually cites a generic clause allowing either party to end the relationship at any time, giving you zero explanation of what triggered the decision.

Having trained bank staff on these exact protocols, I can tell you that the support agent on the phone is not trying to be cruel. First, frontline call center staff are intentionally locked out of the compliance case management system so they cannot accidentally leak investigative details. Second, and far more importantly, bank employees operate under the threat of severe criminal and civil penalties governed by strict anti-"tipping off" laws.

In the United States, the Bank Secrecy Act strictly forbids any bank director, officer, or employee from revealing to a customer that a Suspicious Activity Report has been filed or would reveal the existence of a SAR. As detailed in FinCEN’s official advisory on maintaining SAR confidentiality, unauthorized disclosure is a federal violation carrying civil penalties of up to USD 100,000 per violation and criminal penalties of up to USD 250,000 and five years in prison. In Europe, Article 39 of the EU Anti-Money Laundering Directive (Directive 2015/849) enforces the exact same prohibition against tipping off a customer that their transactions are being analyzed or reported to a Financial Intelligence Unit.

Historically, bank legal departments were so terrified of crossing tipping-off statutes that they instructed staff to say almost nothing during an inquiry. Regulators have recently tried to curb that overreaction; in a September 2026 joint statement on SAR confidentiality and customer communications, FinCEN and federal banking agencies clarified that banks are legally allowed to ask customers factual questions about specific transactions, engage transparently during fraud or account investigations, and communicate account closure decisions without revealing whether a SAR exists. Even so, many compliance departments still default to tight-lipped caution because saying nothing carries zero statutory disclosure risk for the bank.

No legitimate banking setup can guarantee zero compliance alerts, because banks recalibrate their monitoring models constantly and never publish their internal risk thresholds. What you can do is re-architect your financial structure so your cash flows match your declared customer profile, isolate higher-friction payment rails, and give compliance analysts the clean documentation they need to resolve a manual review without escalating toward account closure. Here is the five-step playbook I recommend to independent professionals and remote founders.

Never run your entire financial life through a single bank account. If your client wires, your tax reserves, your crypto off-ramps, and your grocery money all live inside one checking account, a single routine compliance hold can paralyze your ability to pay rent while the review plays out. Build operational firewalls across three distinct banking compartments at separate institutions:

Do not wait for an automated alert to discover that your bank still has you coded as a broke college student. Under the FFIEC’s ongoing Customer Due Diligence framework, banks evaluate higher-risk and cross-border relationships against specific profile attributes: occupation or type of business, source of funds, whether transactions are expected to be domestic or international, and expected transaction volumes. Fintech institutions follow the same logic upfront; Wise’s business verification rules, for example, explicitly collect your business activity details, expected monthly volumes, and counterparty countries, noting that fuller upfront information speeds up verification.

Whenever your career shifts toward self-employment, remote contracting, or higher foreign billings, log into your bank’s profile settings (or schedule a brief call with a relationship manager) before the first big wire arrives. Update your occupation to self-employed or independent consultant, describe your industry in plain terms (such as "B2B software engineering and cloud architecture consulting"), and update your expected monthly deposit range and counterparty regions. Having an updated KYC baseline will not bypass sanctions screening or shield unusual spikes from review, but it directly reduces avoidable alerts caused by outdated onboarding data.

Banks intentionally keep their exact transaction-monitoring lookback windows confidential so bad actors cannot structure transfers around them, whether a given ruleset evaluates 24-hour, 7-day, or 30-day rolling periods. That means there is no magic number of holding days guaranteed to prevent a velocity alert. Even so, treating a deposit account like an instant pass-through pipe is an unforced error.

When a client payment or platform payout lands in your account, resist the urge to sweep 90 percent of it out to an external brokerage, savings platform, or secondary bank within hours of arrival. Leaving a genuine operating reserve in your business account and consolidating outbound owner’s draws, tax set-asides, and brokerage transfers into one or two scheduled moves per month accomplishes two practical goals. First, it keeps your transaction pattern from mimicking the "almost immediately, all or most" onward transfer red flag highlighted in FFIEC Appendix F. Second, maintaining a healthy average balance gives the bank real deposit float to earn net interest income on, improving your standing inside the institution’s account-profitability math.

Payment messages are compliance documents, not chat threads. Under the Bank Secrecy Act’s recordkeeping and Travel Rule requirements detailed in the FFIEC Funds Transfers Recordkeeping manual, institutions handling funds transfers of USD 3,000 or more must retain and transmit specific originator, beneficiary, and payment instruction records. Globally, the Wolfsberg Group’s Payment Transparency Standards and its companion guidance on payment transparency roles and responsibilities emphasize that incomplete or "manifestly meaningless" payment message data impairs sanctions and AML screening and obligates institutions along the chain to monitor for missing details. Directly in FFIEC Appendix F, examiners flag wires that "contain limited content and lack related party information" or show "no apparent links to legitimate contracts, goods, or services."

Require every client to pay against a sequentially numbered PDF invoice showing both legal names, full addresses, a concrete description of the professional services rendered, the billing period, and the exact currency amount. Instruct clients to put a clear, specific reference in the wire remittance field (such as SWIFT MT103 Field 70 or the ISO 20022/SEPA remittance field), for example: "Invoice 2026-104 Cloud Architecture Consulting Oct 2026." A descriptive memo will not prevent an automated rule from firing on a new foreign corridor, and you cannot fix sender data that a third-party payroll processor strips upstream, which is why Step 5 matters. What clean payment references do prevent is avoidable ambiguity during initial alert triage, whereas blank memos, inside jokes, or mislabeling a commercial invoice as a "personal gift" invite immediate escalation.

When a bank or fintech platform sends you a Request for Information (RFI) or pauses a transfer for verification, response windows are often tight. As Wise’s customer verification guide and specialist business verification documentation standards explain, larger transfers, periodic regulatory refreshes, or specific business models routinely prompt specialist teams to pause a transfer or email requests for registration proof, recent bank statements, ownership records, or contracts demonstrating your source of funds. Trying to hunt down year-old agreements and reconcile processor fees while an incoming wire is frozen is a recipe for panic and inconsistent answers.

Create a dedicated, encrypted cloud folder right now and update a ready-to-deploy Compliance Dossier every quarter containing clean PDFs of four core items:

A well-organized PDF package will not override a bank’s risk appetite if an underlying client or jurisdiction violates internal policy. Where it makes a decisive difference is inside the manual workflow: remember McKinsey’s finding that up to 85 percent of bank AML work is bogged down in administrative data gathering. Handing a compliance analyst a single, indexed PDF package that reconciles every deposit to a signed contract and tax record eliminates weeks of back-and-forth document chasing and gives them a complete documentary trail to substantiate a lawful business purpose in their audit file. Doing this quarterly housekeeping also pays off when you apply for a mortgage, where underwriters audit self-employed bank statements with the exact same line-by-line skepticism.

The global economy has moved into the cloud, even if retail banking compliance still runs on 20th-century assumptions. You do not need to shrink your international ambitions or turn down foreign clients to stay banked. You just need to respect the unit economics inside the room, compartmentalize your cash flow, and keep a clean, verifiable paper trail ready whenever the risk engine comes knocking.

Written by Dora Milen, an economist and former commercial banker with 25 years of experience in traditional clearing systems.

"Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

The good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

The IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Important: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

This is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS says "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

Step 3: Calculate the Taxable Amount The actual calculation involves comparing two formulas and taking the lesser amount. For the 50% tier:

Sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:

The remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

The FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

This is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

The math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

For the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

The taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

For single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

No. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

No — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Converting Traditional IRA money to Roth before claiming Social Security can dramatically reduce the tax on your benefits for life.

Yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

Social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

There have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. Plan your retirement income sources deliberately, and you can reduce or eliminate this tax entirely.

#9770. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:

Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:

We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:

Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:

The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:

Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:

The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi does not keep previous reasoning turns while OpenCode and Hermes do, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

Train open models with RL inside real agent harnesses

Explore async reinforcement learning with AsyncGRPOTrainer

#9769. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9768. Token Club: un avatar propio y los primeros trofeos del club

En el primer artículo sobre Token Club conté cómo había pasado de darle vueltas a una idea sobre IA y videojuegos a tener una alfa que se puede probar desde el navegador. Mencioné la tienda y los trofeos, pero me quedé poco en ellos.

Hoy me apetecía enseñarlos con algo más de calma. Son dos partes pequeñas del proyecto, aunque tienen bastante que ver con la experiencia que quiero ir construyendo: elegir cómo apareces dentro del club y guardar un recuerdo de lo que vas haciendo.

Desde Tienda puedes encontrar camisetas, gorras y otros accesorios para el avatar. Las piezas que añades a tu colección pasan al armario de Mi avatar, dentro de Ropa y accesorios.

Hay un detalle que conviene tener en cuenta: añadir una prenda a la colección no cambia automáticamente el aspecto del personaje. Después puedes abrir el armario, probarla y combinarla con lo que ya tienes. Tú eliges qué conjunto quieres llevar.

Si al día siguiente te apetece cambiar, las piezas siguen ahí. Puedes volver a ellas y montar otra combinación. Me gusta esa posibilidad de que el personaje vaya teniendo un poco de tu estilo, aunque solo hayas cambiado una camiseta o una gorra.

Ilustración del armario y la personalización del avatar.

Esta parte también me interesa como prueba de uso. Para quien la está construyendo, el recorrido entre tienda, colección y armario puede parecer evidente. Cuando entra alguien por primera vez, quizá espere que la prenda se equipe directamente o busque sus objetos en otro sitio. Es una de las cosas sobre las que me viene bien recibir comentarios.

La otra parte son los logros. Crear tu primer avatar, guardar un cambio de estilo o conseguir el primer objeto de la tienda son algunos de los pasos que tienen un trofeo asociado.

Puedes consultar la colección desde Trofeos. Allí aparece lo que has conseguido y lo que pide cada logro. Cuando cumples sus requisitos, se desbloquea automáticamente y sale un pequeño aviso; no necesitas ir después a reclamarlo.

La idea es conservar esas primeras veces. Entrar, preparar el personaje, descubrir una prenda y seguir explorando son acciones sencillas, pero ayudan a que la visita tenga algo de recorrido. Tampoco hace falta intentar completar todo de una vez.

Ilustración de los primeros logros y recuerdos del club.

Si te animas a entrar, puedes empezar por algo muy concreto: preparar tu avatar, añadir una pieza de la tienda, buscarla en el armario y elegir cómo combinarla. Después, echar un vistazo a los trofeos para ver qué pasos han quedado registrados.

Me interesa saber si ese recorrido se entiende y si encuentras lo que esperas en cada pantalla. También si alguna prenda se ve mal o si haces una acción que debería desbloquear un logro y no ocurre.

El proyecto sigue en alfa. Quedan ajustes por hacer y los datos de esta etapa podrían reiniciarse. Si algo falla, puedes contármelo en los comentarios o desde el contacto de la web, indicando qué estabas haciendo y qué navegador utilizas.

¿Qué prenda te gustaría encontrar en el armario? ¿Y qué pequeña acción del club crees que merecería tener su propio trofeo?

#9767. Running an Embedding Model Next to My Notes on an iPhone

Independent developer in Punjab, India. Building Hushread (hushread.com), an RSS and news reader with no algorithm.

Independent developer in Punjab, India. Building Hushread (hushread.com), an RSS and news reader with no algorithm.

Independent developer in Punjab, India. Building Hushread (hushread.com), an RSS and news reader with no algorithm.

I keep a lot of notes, and I rarely remember the words I used in them. In March I wrote a note called "Rent split with Arjun". In October I searched for "what does my flatmate owe". Keyword search found nothing, because the two share no words.

So when I built VB Notes, a markdown notes app where every note is a plain .md file in a folder you choose, search by meaning was the part I cared about most. I also wanted it to run on the device. Notes are private, and I wouldn't use a search box that sends every question to a server for my own notes.

This is what it took to run a 350-million-parameter embedding model next to the notes on an iPhone, and the same model on Mac, Windows and Linux.

The phone app is Expo and React Native, and the model runs through react-native-executorch. I wrote 18 questions, each worded differently from the note it should find, and ran them against the models the library ships:

The gap between the right note and an unrelated one mattered more to me than the hit rate. It decides how cleanly you can cut the list off. LFM2.5 became the default, MiniLM is the "Light" choice in Settings, and the multilingual model is there for people who write in more than one language.

LFM2.5 also reads a question and a note differently: questions go in with a query: prefix and notes with document: .

A model reads a limited number of words, so long notes are split into chunks: 200 words each for LFM2.5, each overlapping the previous one by a fifth, at most 16 per note. Every chunk starts with the note's title, so a paragraph deep inside "Trip to Ladakh" still knows it is about the trip.

Code blocks and Mermaid diagrams are left out. They are noise for meaning, and keyword search still finds them. Tags lose their # and count as words, so #work/clients still says what the note is about.

Each chunk becomes 1,024 numbers. As float32 that is 4 KB per chunk. I store each vector as int8 with one float32 scale in front: a quarter of the size, and the cosine similarity barely moves.

The vectors live in a SQLite file in the app's caches folder, out of iCloud backups. If iOS clears it, the app embeds the notes again. The .md files are always the source of truth.

At launch the app reads only each note's hash, to see what changed. The vectors load on the first search and stay in memory. The model itself waits three seconds after launch, unless you open Search first, so opening the app stays quick.

Cosine scores from a small model are not probabilities. A fixed floor of 0.3 sounded reasonable and dropped most of the right answers: short questions score between 0.15 and 0.3 even against the note they are about.

What works is two rules. Each model gets its own floor, at the level where unrelated notes stop (0.12 for LFM2.5). And a match is kept only if it is within 0.25 of the best match, up to ten matches.

Exact words still matter. If I type "Diamox", I want the note that says "Diamox" first. Keyword search is SQLite FTS5 on word starts, so "gro" finds "Groceries".

The two lists are merged with reciprocal rank fusion: a note scores 1 / (60 + its rank) in each list, and the scores add up. A note found by both rises to the top, and a note found only by meaning still shows. I never have to compare a keyword score with a cosine score, which would be comparing two different things.

On the desktop, a single word only brings in meaning matches when no note contains it. One word gives the model little to go on, and the exact matches are what you want.

The first surprise was the download. I expected an iOS background download to be the right tool. On the simulator, the app's own download ran at 2.4 MB/s, while an iOS background session managed 0.05 to 0.9 MB/s.

So the download runs inside the app. The screen stays awake while it runs, and if you leave the app it stops, then carries on from the partial file when you come back.

The desktop app is Tauri 2 with Rust, not Electron. It uses the same model, as the official Q8_0 GGUF file (380 MB, checked by SHA-256 and downloaded on first launch), run by llama.cpp through the llama-cpp-2 crate: on Metal on Apple Silicon, on the CPU elsewhere, on its own thread.

Notes are chunked by the same TypeScript code as on the phone, and a background thread embeds them newest first, so recent notes become searchable first. The same chunks and the same model mean a question finds the same notes on both.

Try it: VB Notes is free and open source (MIT), for iPhone, Android, Mac, Windows and Linux. There is no account and no server: notes stay plain files, and search runs on your phone or computer.

I'd like to hear how you handle search in your own notes, and what would make you trust a model running next to them.

How I Fold Thirty Reports of the Same Event Into One Story
