#9766. Auditable Node.js Cron Cleanup: Expired Sessions, Tokens, Queues, Redis TTL, Webhooks

Short answer: use a cron trigger to create a bounded cleanup job, let a queue consumer process it in small PostgreSQL transactions, and make the database receipt the authority for completion. Redis TTL can remove a second lookup path, but it should not be the only record when a customer-support system must explain which expired session or token was removed and why.

The important distinction is between scheduling and delivery. A cron expression says when to ask for work; it does not say that old user sessions were deleted, that expired tokens were visited, or that a public webhook was delivered exactly once. For a backend that handles support events, a retry is normal traffic, not an exceptional event. The design therefore needs an exactly-once effect even though the trigger, webhook, and queue each provide at-least-once delivery.

The cleanup job should carry a deterministic job_id, an expiry cutoff, and a bounded scope such as a tenant or primary-key interval. It should not carry a snapshot of every row selected for deletion. The scheduler or public webhook authenticates the request, records the intent, and enqueues that small description. A worker reads the description, selects rows from PostgreSQL using the stored expires_at, deletes a batch, inserts a receipt in the same transaction, and acknowledges the queue message only after commit.

That sequence gives every stage a failure boundary. A process may die before enqueueing, after enqueueing, after the database commit, or after the queue acknowledgement. The receipt makes the third case harmless: a redelivery finds the completed job_id and records no second deletion. The database remains the authority for expiry and completion, while the queue is responsible for carrying work.

Three words: receipt before acknowledgement.

The first version should be report-only. Record the cutoff, candidate count, tenant, and range, then compare those results with an independent query for several runs before enabling destructive deletes. I would also keep the request ID, queue message ID, worker attempt, committed count, and completion time in an audit trail; a green cron history is too small an explanation for a deletion that a support agent may need to defend later.

The trade-offs are architectural, not cosmetic:

There is no universal winner. Choose the smallest mechanism that preserves the evidence your retention and compliance rules require.

Keep the Node.js HTTP handler boring. It validates the method and authentication, computes a cutoff from a trusted clock, creates an idempotency key, and returns only after the job is durably queued. It should not scan a user-session table or wait for the queue consumer to delete anything. A public webhook endpoint is a trigger surface, not a worker.

The endpoint's response also needs a precise meaning. 202 Accepted can mean that the bounded job was durably accepted; it must not be presented as proof that cleanup finished. If enqueueing cannot be confirmed, return a failure that causes the caller to retry, and make that retry resolve to the same job_id. Never derive the idempotency key from a random request ID if two cron invocations for the same cutoff should represent one cleanup run.

An old session and an expired token deserve the same expiry discipline, although they need not share a table or delete transaction. The worker can process each relation in bounded batches, record separate counts, and advance a cursor. If a tenant has a large backlog, enqueue the next cursor as a continuation job. That keeps locks short and gives operators a visible unit of progress.

Redis TTL is useful for making a session unavailable quickly. It is a poor audit log: key eviction does not by itself provide the business context of who requested cleanup, which cutoff was applied, or whether a token was also revoked in PostgreSQL. Treat TTL as a serving optimization or a safety net; persist the policy decision where reconciliation can query it.

The following Go sketch shows the critical path without tying it to a queue product. publish and next are adapters. The correctness contract is the same for a Redis-backed queue, a database-backed queue, or a managed queue: the worker commits the receipt before it acknowledges delivery.

The SQL is a sketch, not a claim that every PostgreSQL deployment accepts a LIMIT directly on DELETE; use the database's supported bounded-delete form, normally a keyset-selected subquery, and test it against the schema and indexes you actually run. That detail matters because a correct idempotency key does not protect a transaction that locks the entire table. I have seen teams spend a day proving duplicate suppression while the real incident was a cleanup query that held locks past the webhook timeout.

The receipt should include the cutoff and useful scope fields, with a unique constraint on job_id. If sessions and tokens are handled separately, use distinct receipt kinds or separate rows so a retry can determine exactly which work committed. A worker crash after commit but before Ack is the test that proves the design; the second delivery must do no destructive work.

Run the failure matrix before production:

The monitoring should distinguish accepted triggers, queued jobs, worker attempts, committed receipts, and rows still expired. Those signals answer different questions. A successful webhook with an empty receipt stream means “the trigger worked,” not “the cleanup worked.”

Cron also has a semantic limit: it supplies a time-based invocation, not a durable history of all work that a service forgot to perform. A paused schedule may not recreate every missed invocation, so the job table or queue must provide replay and the operator must know how to issue a bounded backfill. If the business rule requires durable timers, multi-step state, or compensation, a workflow engine is a better boundary than a clever cron expression.

Don't promise exactly-once delivery to a downstream customer-support endpoint. Promise an exactly-once effect inside your own cleanup ledger, and give downstream webhook consumers their own idempotency key. The distinction is small in wording and large in an audit.

I would reject a single cron command that runs DELETE for every expired session and token, then reports success from the scheduler. It has no durable handoff, no stable replay unit, and no reliable way to tell “nothing was due” from “the process stopped halfway.” It is acceptable only for a small, disposable table whose loss can be rebuilt and whose deletion needs no audit trail; that is not the usual posture for customer-support sessions or authentication tokens.

I would also reject Redis TTL as the complete retention policy when PostgreSQL is the system of record. TTL is a good answer to fast invalidation, and it can reduce read pressure, but it cannot replace a receipt with scope, cutoff, and operator-visible reconciliation. Use it alongside the authoritative store when latency matters.

The final decision rule is direct: use cron for the nudge, a queue for bounded delivery, PostgreSQL for expiry and receipts, and Redis TTL only where fast serving behavior justifies a second mechanism. If the workload becomes a workflow graph or needs replayable event history, choose a workflow engine or an event log instead. Your mileage will vary with table size, retention law, and network topology; those constraints should change the design, not be hidden behind a green schedule.

#9765. How I Traced a Missing Vercel AI SDK Duration Histogram

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I could see how long the model call took in an OpenTelemetry span. My metrics export showed a counter I’d added during the same run. I looked for the inference duration histogram and came up empty. The counter told me the metrics exporter worked.

I filed AI SDK issue #24229 with the reproduction. The histogram shipped in @ai-sdk/otel 1.0.160 through PR #24354. That gave me a way to check what gen_ai.client.inference.duration actually measures.

I ran 25 calls on each version, five each for three generation delays, a stream and an error. A local mock model supplied the delays with timers, and I flushed the in-memory export after every call. The older version recorded zero histogram observations. The new version recorded 25, including all five errors.

I started with ai 7.0.157 and @ai-sdk/otel 1.0.157. The reproduction printed this:

An empty export could have sent me back to the exporter setup. Seeing repro.control gave me a reason to look at the integration first.

The duration I saw was gen_ai.client.operation.duration, an attribute on the span. To query the distribution I needed the integration to emit a histogram.

The span and the histogram take separate paths. A TracerProvider sends spans to a span exporter. The metric needs a MeterProvider, a reader and a metric exporter.

In my reproduction I registered new OpenTelemetry() before setting the global meter provider. That order works with the shipped code because it looks up the meter when it records the duration.

I pinned ai and @ai-sdk/otel at 7.0.157 and 1.0.157 for the first run, then 7.0.160 and 1.0.160 for the second configuration. Both used OpenTelemetry API 1.9.1, metrics SDK 2.8.0, trace SDK 2.7.1 and Node 24.22.2.

Both configurations ran on the same Linux server. Within each one I called MockLanguageModelV4 sequentially and flushed after each attempt. I disabled retries and left CPU and network settings alone.

Wait 40 ms, emit text, wait 160 ms, finish

An 80 ms timer can run a little late. I wanted to see the groups separate in the export, so I used delays far enough apart to see that.

The in-memory exporter let me read the measurements directly. Here’s how I set it up after registering tracing and the integration.

I incremented repro.control and flushed after every attempt. The issue reproduction has the tracing setup and mock model. To repeat the comparison, pin both AI SDK packages together.

Both counters ended at 25. Version 1.0.157 exported no inference histogram. Version 1.0.160 exported a histogram with 25 observations.

After each call, I subtracted the previous cumulative sum for the same attribute set, checking that its count had increased by one. That gave me a duration in seconds for that call. I converted the medians to milliseconds for the table.

The three generation groups landed close to their timer delays. The stream and the errors contributed their own measurements.

I had the mock wait 40 ms, emit text, then wait another 160 ms before closing. The caller consumed all of textStream.

First text reached my caller at a median of 43.6 ms across five calls. The histogram recorded a median of 202.3 ms for the full invocation. Those clocks start in different places, so I’d track time to first text as its own measurement.

For future reproductions I’d save the GenAI semantic convention revision alongside the package versions.

The failing mock waited 80 ms and threw Error('controlled failure'). All five attempts were recorded with retries disabled.

I want to see those failures when I’m checking latency. The PR and its tests also cover cancellation and failed stream attempts during retries. My test exercised a thrown error.

The count is model attempts. One user action can cause several model calls, and retries can add more attempts. Local tool execution time is outside this duration.

The error point had the operation and requested model alongside error.type. The provider was normalized from openai.chat to openai. The point can also carry a response model when the integration has one.

I chose the model IDs as labels for the mock groups. The exported point had no prompt or response text.

The updated integration docs show that telemetry.isEnabled: false turns off metrics for the call. The payload controls recordInputs and recordOutputs leave duration recording on. This histogram comes from the new integration.

I flushed after each attempt and chose cumulative aggregation. By the fifth flush, the snapshot for that group already included the previous four calls.

The export puts bucket counts into discrete intervals. I’d check how my backend represents them before writing a percentile query. The integration suggests boundaries in seconds, and the metrics SDK can override them.

I’d start the same way on a real service. Check the control counter and one successful call, then read the metric name, unit, attributes, count and sum in the export. Try one failed call and let one stream close. I would have missed that last 160 ms if I’d stopped reading at the first chunk.

#9764. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. Once you compare these benefits to what you get with other platforms such as Shopify, you should find that it is worth your time to consider sellfy for your business. #9763. eMondrian now speaks JSON: a REST API on your semantic model

Posted on Nov 20 • Originally published at docs.emondrian.com

Until now, a program that wanted numbers from eMondrian had to speak XMLA: SOAP envelopes, XML answers, a client library that exists for few languages. Excel and Power BI do this for you. A Python script, a Node backend or an n8n workflow don't.

From Community 2026.11.20 eMondrian also answers over REST with JSON. Send an MDX or DAX query in a POST request and get rows back:

You can run this request yourself: it goes to our public demo, 182 million US flights in ClickHouse, open without sign-in. The answer took 168 ms.

A semantic model defines your numbers once: what Revenue is, how Margin is calculated, which rows each customer may see. Excel, Power BI and AI agents already use it. Now everything else can, too, and gets the same numbers.

With an AI agent anyone can build a dashboard page in their own design in minutes. The hard part is the data behind it: the agent writes the numbers into the file, or the page gets a database password.

With the REST API, the page's backend asks eMondrian for the data at each view:

The data is live, the file holds no numbers, and the database password stays in eMondrian. The measures are the model's: Unit Sales on the page is the same number as in Excel.

Give each customer an eMondrian user and a role. An administrator issues that user's personal token, on the page /account/tokens?user=acme-portal or from a script:

The answer shows the token once. Your backend keeps it and calls the API with it, and the server filters the rows:

Same query, same code. With an administrator's token the answer has three states; with Acme's token, only Oregon. With rollupPolicy="partial" on the role's grant, totals count only the rows the role allows. The filter is not in your JavaScript, so nobody can remove it in the browser.

A user has one personal token, so give the portal a user of its own: revoking its token stops nothing else. To take access away, revoke the token or disable the user: the token stops working within 30 seconds.

A data scientist doesn't need an XMLA library to get the official numbers:

A DAX query names the cube, and its columns are named as in the query: Store[Store State] and [Unit Sales]. The forecast in the notebook starts from the same Unit Sales as the board report.

n8n, Make, Retool, Zapier, a Power Automate flow: any tool that can send an HTTP request and read JSON can now query the model. A few ideas:

A scheduled job reads aggregates from the model and writes them where they are needed: a CRM field with each account's revenue, a planning sheet, a partner's file. The numbers in the export are the model's, not another SQL query that someone wrote once and nobody checks.

By default a request returns up to 10,000 rows; it can ask for up to 100,000 with maxRows. Both limits are server settings, and truncated says when rows were left out.

An agent that writes code reads /api/v1/openapi.json, signed in with the service's credentials, and knows the whole API. It reads the cube's model from /api/v1/catalogs/{catalog}/cubes/{cube} and writes queries in business names: Unit Sales, Store State, not tables and joins. The service it writes runs as a user with a role, so it sees only what that user may see.

#9761. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing.

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9760. How Four Evaluation Bugs Distorted a Cross-Encoder Model Comparison

CTO & CPO | Enterprise AI & Big Data at National Scale

CTO & CPO | Enterprise AI & Big Data at National Scale

CTO & CPO | Enterprise AI & Big Data at National Scale

My first comparison of two releases showed a clean accuracy gain and two large regressions. None of the three was real. Fixing that took four bugs. Once the numbers were right, half of my wording benchmark turned out not to be held out, and a conclusion I nearly published came from comparing effects measured at different candidate-set sizes.

I maintain Ru-Jev, an open typed-decision model for Russian-language text. It takes a context and a set of candidate options and returns a probability for each option. It does not generate text. Technically, it is a pointwise cross-encoder on mmBERT-base, 307M parameters: each (context, option) pair gets its own encoder pass, and a softmax over the options gives the distribution. It runs on CPU, so it can sit inside a closed network. Weights and code are MIT.

Version 1.3 had one goal. The caller names the options, in the caller's own words, and version 1.1 had learned the exact label wordings in its training data. So 1.3 presents each label in several surface forms during training, including English intent keys transliterated into Cyrillic and a clipped form of that transliteration, and draws one form per example.

The first table had two regressions I could not explain. Sentence acceptability fell from 0.909 to 0.647. A reasoning set fell from 0.939 to 0.596. A release that only changed label wording had no mechanism for that.

The data builder carved each task's validation slice like this:

random.shuffle with no generator draws from the module-level stream, which every other random call in the file also consumes, including the new choice of label wording. Adding label styles to one task changed how many draws happened before the next task was carved, and every later task got a different split.

That is leakage, and it can be measured: 90.3% of 1.3's acceptability validation rows and 89.4% of its reasoning rows had been in 1.1's training data. The 0.909 was 1.1 scored on rows it had trained on. On held-out rows it scores 0.650.

The fix seeds each carve from the task name:

The check is what confirms the diagnosis. I rebuilt the previous release's data from its commit and confirmed that the six tasks whose option sets never changed matched at 100%. Those tasks had no reason to move, so if they had moved, my diagnosis would have been wrong.

With the split repaired I matched the two validation sets by input text and found nine comparable tasks. In this release a row with the same text can carry an option wording 1.1 never saw, so scoring 1.1 on it measures robustness to renaming, not accuracy. Matching on text and option wording together leaves six tasks.

A toxicity gain from 0.722 to 0.954 that I had presented as a capability gain was this bug. Version 1.1 scores 0.961 on toxicity with the labels it trained on.

The summary row of my comparison table, 0.7948 against 0.7920 on 5,078 decisions, came from one random half of the comparable rows. The per-task table beside it counted all 10,157. A calibration advantage, 0.0172 against 0.0160, came from the same single split. Both numbers reached the published model card.

On all 10,157 rows the two releases answer exactly 8,120 correctly, disagreeing on 1,680 rows split 840 and 840. Over 25 random splits the calibration difference changes sign. Both claims were withdrawn. What survives is narrower: 1.3 takes a lower fitted temperature in all 25 splits, so its raw scores are less overconfident, but after each model gets its own temperature the residual calibration error is the same.

To measure seed variance I retrained both recipes on a rented GPU and checked the data on the remote machine against my local copy by SHA-256, row count and per-task counts. Everything matched. The local copy predated the commit that added the transliteration styles, so the "augmented" seed runs were trained without the augmentation. Their jargon accuracy fell in the baseline's range, and I first read that as an unstable recipe.

Row counts could not catch it, because the new styles change option strings, not the number of rows. What caught it was counting distinct option strings per task: 120 in the stale copy, 198 after rebuilding. Those runs are excluded from everything.

Once the numbers were right, I ran a wider wording test: ten label vocabularies on the same 1,000 routing questions, each scored with five candidates per question and eight of them also with all eighteen. Because the model scores every option independently, the five-candidate answer can be computed exactly from the eighteen-candidate run. I checked every probe label against all training option strings, used exact McNemar tests, a bootstrap that resamples labels rather than just questions, and a Holm correction over 23 comparisons.

Two things came out of it. First, two of my six original benchmark vocabularies, the English key and the ordinary Russian word, turned out to be training styles for both releases, and a third, the Russian phrase, was a training style for the new release only. Half of my original benchmark was not a held-out test.

Second, the effect size depended on the number of candidates, differently for different vocabularies. I had first measured jargon with five candidates and slang with eighteen, which made the slang gain look far smaller than the jargon gain. With both vocabularies in both settings:

English-derived jargon, strict (no exact or prefix match to training)

Department names (no exact match; 2 of 18 labels share a prefix with a training option)

On every held-out vocabulary made of words, the new release is better in both settings, though not every gain survives the Holm correction. On abbreviations and opaque codes there is no usable gain. The two releases differ in more than the augmentation (I also fixed the split and trained four epochs instead of three), so this compares two trained models rather than a clean ablation. Two replicates of the v1.1 recipe scored 0.658 and 0.622 on jargon with five candidates, against 0.633 for the release, so small differences in the table should not be read as reproducible; the jargon gains are large relative to that spread. The contrast I almost published between jargon and slang came from comparing a five-candidate effect with an eighteen-candidate one.

Accuracy and confidence also diverged. Where accuracy rose, the risk–coverage curve mostly improved, but with eighteen candidates the number of wrong answers given above 0.8 confidence went up on jargon (all labels, 79 to 109 per 1,000) and on slang, because the new release is more confident overall. On department names it went down.

Author’s note: The name references Jev, a commercial decision model by TypeSafe AI. Ru-Jev is an independent project, not affiliated with TypeSafe AI and not trained on Jev outputs.

#9759. Node.js Browser Storage: 5 Presigned URL Upload Choices for SaaS

Tenant isolation matters more than the storage logo. Short answer: issue short-lived presigned PUT and GET URLs from your Node.js backend, derive every object key on the server, and keep the bucket private. For generated property reports, start with the option whose CORS controls, authorization model, and cleanup behavior you can verify before the first upload.

My recommendation is conditional, not fashionable. Use AWS S3 when the team wants direct ownership of storage configuration. Evaluate R2 when S3 compatibility is strategically useful. Put Supabase Storage or UploadThing first when either already defines the application's upload layer. The last option fits a team that values discovering and wiring a capability from one REST surface, but only when CORS is already compatible and permanent public URLs are unnecessary.

A UUID makes a key difficult to guess. It does not prove that customer A may write or read customer B's report. The backend must obtain the authenticated tenant identifier, validate the report identifier against that tenant, and then construct the storage key itself. Never accept a complete object key from the browser.

A useful shape is tenants/{tenantId}/reports/{reportId}/{fileId}.pdf. The exact punctuation is boring. Good. The security property is that tenantId comes from the authenticated server session, not a form field, while fileId prevents an accidental overwrite. Store the key with the report record and authorize each later download against that record.

Presigned URLs are bearer credentials. Keep their lifetime short, constrain the operation to PUT or GET, and return them only after authorization. Do not log the query string. A private GET URL should be minted after every download check; it should not become a permanent link copied into invoices or emails.

This is the first benchmark I care about: count the places where a browser-supplied tenant or key can cross the trust boundary. The target is zero. Latency numbers can wait. My first instinct with upload tooling is usually to compare time-to-first-call. Here that is incomplete. A five-minute setup that trusts a client-provided tenant key has failed the important test, while a slightly longer integration that derives the key after authorization has the better developer experience because its security rule is visible in one place.

Browser direct upload crosses two enforcement systems. The signed URL authorizes storage. CORS decides whether browser JavaScript may make that cross-origin request. A valid signature does not repair a missing Access-Control-Allow-Origin response.

Test the exact production origin, method, and request headers. PUT plus Content-Type usually causes a preflight request, so the storage service must answer that OPTIONS exchange correctly. Avoid * when the workflow uses credentials or exposes more origins than intended. MDN's CORS guide is the useful baseline here.

This criterion changes the shortlist. S3 exposes a documented bucket configuration surface. R2, Supabase Storage, and UploadThing should each be checked against the team's actual origin and framework rather than accepted on the strength of a compatibility label. The self-describing REST option's storage model contains CORS rules, but self-service CORS configuration is not available through the API for this workflow. If the property portal's origin is not already allowed, browser direct upload can stop there.

Sharp edge. Test preflight before implementing progress bars.

The browser needs an application endpoint that returns a short-lived upload URL. It does not need a storage credential, a bucket name chosen by the user, or permission to list objects. The following TypeScript calls the verified presign route from a trusted Node.js process. Its base URL, key, bucket, and server-derived object key come from the environment; the response is preserved as JSON because the supplied contract does not establish a narrower response type.

The object key passed to that process should have the server-derived tenants/{tenantId}/reports/... shape. The capability's discovery document supplies its full request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so use those schemas to consume the returned grant rather than guessing fields. Then measure time-to-first-byte and completed-upload rate with realistic report sizes. Also verify that the signed constraints and the browser's Content-Type agree byte for byte. That mismatch is a much more useful test than another abstraction layer.

For a self-describing API, discovery shortens the adapter work: one capability response provides the full request schema, response schema, billing metadata, and runnable examples. Infrai covers 295 routes across 20 modules with a single API key and a single bill, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. For a property platform that also calls other backend services, one key avoids adding another credential format; one bill removes a separate reconciliation path. Those gains matter after the upload works, not before. They do not remove the need to test CORS or tenant authorization.

Use single-request PUT for ordinary generated PDFs until measurements show it is inadequate. Multipart upload adds state: an upload ID, numbered parts, completion, and abort. AWS documents that uploaded parts continue consuming storage until the upload is completed or aborted. The same cleanup discipline matters for any provider that exposes multipart state.

With this storage capability, orphaned multipart parts are not cleaned automatically. Record the upload ID in a job table. On success, complete it explicitly; on cancellation or timeout, abort it. A periodic reconciler can find application jobs left in an uploading state, but prefix listing cannot query arbitrary metadata, so the database remains the source of cleanup intent.

Retries need narrower rules than “try again.” A failed presign request can be retried with backoff. A 429 response should honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff. A completed write should not be blindly repeated; use a stable client-supplied identifier or an idempotency key where the API supports it. There is no If-Match conditional write here, so strict concurrent replacement of the same report key needs a database transaction or queue.

Choose direct AWS S3 when detailed bucket CORS control and the documented multipart lifecycle are requirements your team is prepared to operate. Choose R2 when your architecture explicitly benefits from an S3-compatible target and its verified behavior meets the same preflight and private-download tests. I first thought compatibility would settle most of the decision. It doesn't. Compatibility reduces client changes; it does not prove identical policy semantics, tenant authorization, or a passing browser preflight from the production origin.

Supabase Storage is the more coherent runner-up for a product already centered on Supabase, provided its authorization rules pass cross-tenant tests. UploadThing deserves the same treatment in an application that wants an upload-focused integration rather than a general object API. In both cases, benchmark time-to-first-successful upload, configuration count, and the number of authorization decisions duplicated outside the application database. I would reject any option that makes those decisions hard to locate, even if its happy-path demo is shorter.

These limitations are decisive. The capability compared here is not suitable for static hosting, an image host, or any design that requires a permanent public object URL: public and public-read ACLs are unavailable, and public_url remains null. It also does not support object versioning or object lock, so it cannot recover an overwritten key or provide WORM guarantees by itself. Cross-region automatic replication and bulk cross-cloud migration are outside its scope. Lifecycle expiry starts at one day, not hours. The trade-off is clear: choose AWS S3 instead when those native controls are requirements, and choose a product-specific upload layer when reducing application integration matters more than a general storage API.

Those are architecture boundaries. For authenticated property reports, private presigned GETs are often the right behavior anyway. For public assets, regulated immutable records, active-active regional copies, or metadata-heavy search, pick a storage system designed around that requirement and prove it with an integration test before migrating data.

#9758. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

#9757. The Holiday Shopping Season Is Here. Are Consumers Ready to Trust AI Assistants?

Joanna is a Head of Consumer Research and Marketing at PissedConsumer.com.

Joanna is a Head of Consumer Research and Marketing at PissedConsumer.com.

Joanna is a Head of Consumer Research and Marketing at PissedConsumer.com.

Businesses are investing heavily in AI shopping assistants, yet consumers remain hesitant. Why does shopper enthusiasm for AI additions to the shopping journey appear to be trailing behind that of retailers?

A recent survey of holiday shopping trends finds that only 9.9% of consumers intend to use AI tools in their 2026 holiday shopping plans, while 52.2% completely rule out using AI at all.

According to Adobe's holiday shopping research, AI-driven traffic to US retailers' websites will grow 130% in the 2026 holiday shopping season, but this increase is still modest compared with traditional advertising and other channels. So while there is an uptick in AI involvement in seasonal shopping, it’s still not quite in the realm of mainstream adoption, so expectations for AI-driven revenue should be tempered accordingly.

Unsurprisingly, as AI excels at sifting and retrieving relevant data from vast amounts of information, comparing products and prices is the standout use case here. In the holiday shopping survey among PissedConsumer’s users in four countries, respondents who say they use AI shopping tools cite comparison as their number one benefit, at 27.9%. Helping to draw up personalized shopping lists and sourcing discount codes are also ways these tools boost buyer confidence.

From the retailer's perspective, an AI assistant that shortlists 100 items into five top contenders brings time-saving value to the customer, whereas distractions and unnecessarily complicated processes will make the checkout feel more distant.

Misleading, irrelevant, or just plain wrong information causes shoppers to turn away from AI assistants. According to other research, shoppers try an average of only three prompts before giving up on AI recommendations, and 32% blame AI for poor recommendations if they are unsatisfied with the results of the search.

An AI tool can only ever be as good as the data it works with, so keep all information that it depends on, such as prices, inventory counts, return windows, etc., accurate, up to date, and synchronized with your storefront. Inaccurate details will guarantee complaints, cancellations, and lost customers.

Focus investment in areas that have proven worth to consumers. Comparisons and gift ideas are high-value to shoppers and low-risk applications. Be conscious of AI agent limitations and, when these are reached, enable an easy handover to a human customer service agent.

And finally, test and track performance. Just because clicks are going up doesn’t mean customer trust is following. The goal is to nurture consumer confidence.

The consumer data portrays a curious but cautious customer. Even though about one in four consumers might use an AI shopping assistant this holiday, it’s not a sign of significant growth or widespread adoption.

Smart implementation could be the answer. Retailers that lead with robust, proven AI tools that fix fundamental bottlenecks or resolve customer uncertainty, even in small or subtle ways, will build customer confidence, turning curiosity into repeated use of such tools.

The 2026 holiday shopping season is an opportunity to show your customers that you can save them time, money, and stress. Build trust in December, and you’ll have a strong platform for success when adoption finally does take off.

#9756. Telemetry clues for a CVE-2026-123634 investigation

There is no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-123634 in the reviewed sources, so telemetry cannot be reduced to a signature for a known campaign. Investigators need signals that map to the resolver, memory corruption, DNS requirements, and worker execution path. Each signal has benign explanations and needs correlation.

CVE-2026-123634 is an NGINX resolver use-after-free affecting Open Source versions 0.6.18 through 1.31.8. The fix is in 1.31.9 and 1.30.7. The CVE is classified as CWE-416 and scored 9.2 under CVSS v4.0.

The vulnerability can terminate a worker during a failed exploit attempt. A successful attempt can turn the resolver callback path into worker-level code execution. The public research describes a tested proof and does not report a live intrusion.

Nginx launches resolver work when proxy_pass refers to a request-derived name that needs DNS. A mirror subrequest can create a second context for the same name. When DNS processing returns, the main request can fail to send its 502 response because the client reset the connection. Request cleanup then frees the mirror context while the resolver loop still holds a pointer to it.

The attacker needs control over the DNS answer path, such as an authoritative DNS server that nginx's resolver reaches. The HTTP request must reach a vulnerable route and create the required cleanup sequence. The final impact depends on memory reclamation and callback control. This is more specific than a generic malformed-request attempt, and logs may not retain the fields needed to prove or exclude it.

A failed attempt may appear as a crash, a burst of failed upstream requests, or resolver errors. A successful attempt may produce no obvious alert if the worker remains running long enough to execute commands. The strongest host signal is a child process launched by the nginx worker account, based on Xint's detection guidance. That event needs investigation even though unrelated scripts can run under the same account in some environments.

The version range is 0.6.18 through 1.31.8 before the fixed releases. The investigation scope also depends on configuration and network reachability. Check servers with resolver directives, variable proxy destinations, and mirror or SSI subrequests first, then extend to all systems that run an unpatched package because an inventory may be incomplete.

Distribution backports can make a vulnerable-looking version fixed, and a missing package from a vendor table is not proof of safety. Verify the full package version and the vendor advisory. Include container images and infrastructure-as-code definitions in the review.

ZoomEye Search app="NGINX" returned 316,220,816 product fingerprints. Filter vul.cve="CVE-2026-123634" returned 0. The product count is not evidence that an individual endpoint used the vulnerable resolver path or that it was attacked. Exposure work should be joined with DNS egress records and configuration inventories.

Patch to 1.31.9, 1.30.7, or a later maintained release. For temporary containment, use fixed upstream groups instead of request-time DNS lookup and remove unnecessary mirroring. Validate the configuration and worker replacement. Preserve logs before restarting or rebuilding a potentially compromised host.

Practical review items include unexpected nginx worker exits, signal 11 or segfault messages, bursts of 502 responses, resolver errors, and new child processes under the worker account. Correlate these with DNS queries to unusual domains, client resets, and the relevant nginx routes. An empty log search cannot prove that no exploitation occurred because ordinary access logs may omit resolver context and connection-level detail.

#9755. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9754. AI coding assistant vs AI coding agent: what is the difference?

An AI coding assistant helps while you write: it suggests the next lines, explains code and answers questions, and you do the work. An AI coding agent takes a whole task: it reads your project, changes the files, runs the commands that check the work and fixes what fails, while you approve and review. This guide explains the difference, when each one is the right tool, and how to keep an agent under control. We use Mel – the agentic terminal (openmel.dev), the agentic team for coding, in the examples.

An AI coding assistant is a helper that sits next to you while you code.

It comes in two common forms. One is autocomplete: you type, and it offers the next line or the rest of the function. The other is a chat box: you paste code or ask a question, and it answers with an explanation or a snippet.

Either way, you stay the one who does the work. You decide which file to open, you copy the answer in, you run the build, and you read the error. The assistant makes each step faster. It does not take the steps for you.

An AI coding agent is a tool you hand a task to, not a question.

You describe what you want: "fix the failing date test and do not touch the API." The agent reads the code it needs, makes a plan, edits the files, runs the test command, reads the output and tries again if the test still fails. When it is done, it shows you what changed.

The key word is loop. An agent can act, look at the result of its action and decide the next step. That is what lets it finish a task with several steps instead of answering one prompt at a time.

An agentic coding desktop app such as Mel goes one step further: a team of agents works on files, commands, code and diff review, so planning, building and checking are not all left to one chat.

When you already know what to do and want to do it faster.

If the task fits on one screen and you will run the check yourself anyway, an assistant is often all you need.

When the task has more steps than you want to do by hand.

A simple rule: if you would write the task down for a colleague, it is an agent task. If you would just type it, an assistant is enough.

It is, if you stay in control of what it runs and what it changes.

An agent is more useful than an assistant because it can act. That is also why it needs more care. Three habits cover most of the risk:

A common split: the assistant for the small edits you make while you read code, and the agent for the task you would otherwise spend an afternoon on.

What matters is that each tool fits your workflow. If your team works in VS Code, check that the agent works there too. If your team uses Mac, Windows and Linux, check that one tool covers all three.

Mel – the agentic terminal is a multi-agent, multi-model AI terminal and an agentic coding app for Mac and Windows, and for Linux and VS Code too. It plans, builds, tests and ships your work, from prompt to production-ready code, with you in control, and it is building the first superintelligent terminal.

In Mel, a team of agents works on files, commands, code and diff review. You choose the model for each task: Mel works with Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek and Qwen, US and Chinese models in one tool.

Mel is free with your own API key. Pro is $20 a month and Max is $200 a month. For teams, Mel Business has shared credits and one invoice, at $50 a seat with 2 seats minimum.

To try an agent on a real task, download Mel, turn approvals on and give it one small bug with a test. If you want to walk through it with your team, write to hello@openmel.dev and we will set up a short demo.

What is the difference between an AI coding assistant and an AI coding agent? An assistant suggests code and answers questions while you do the work. An agent takes a task, changes the files, runs the commands that check the work and fixes what fails, while you approve and review.

Is an AI coding agent better than an AI coding assistant? Not always. An agent is better for tasks with several steps and a clear finish line. An assistant is often faster for small edits you already know how to make.

Does an AI coding agent replace a developer? No. You still decide the task, approve what it runs and review the diff before anything is kept. The agent does the steps in between.

Is there a free AI coding agent? Yes. Mel is free with your own API key on Mac, Windows and Linux, plus a VS Code extension.

#9753. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9752. Why AI Agents Leave You More Tired, Not More Rested

Co-founder of DOITONG & HashEx. Expert in AI, blockchain security, and product strategy.

Co-founder of DOITONG & HashEx. Expert in AI, blockchain security, and product strategy.

Co-founder of DOITONG & HashEx. Expert in AI, blockchain security, and product strategy.

It sounds like AI agents should leave us rested. They take routine work off our hands, so we should have more time and more energy. In practice, I hear the opposite more and more often: “I used to sit through the whole workday. Now by lunch I can only stare at the wall.”

Personally, I think the explanation comes from the agents themselves. Let’s look at a person the way we look at an agent: as something with a context window.

Look at how work used to be. A developer adds a button to a website. Their head is busy with one domain: the interface, the programming language, the framework. A good manager knew this and gave each person tasks where they were strong and fast.

Now an agent adds the button. The person only gives the task. Meanwhile, other agents write articles, draw designs, make videos, and run research. Instead of a frontend developer, a backend developer and a product manager, we have one product builder who orchestrates agents: marketing, product, development, hotfixes, calls with the business owners. And then someone sends a personal question in the chat.

Researchers at UC Berkeley saw the same at a tech company that gave everyone AI tools: people took on tasks that used to belong to others (Berkeley Haas).

Imagine a map. Before, a person’s brain moved around one city. A senior specialist moved around a country. Now the brain travels between continents several times a day, and every trip costs far more than a ride across town. Is it just more work? No. It is much more expensive work.

There is a second problem. In our home domain, the roads are built: we have walked them a thousand times. Between domains, the brain often walks a new path. That takes time and energy, and by the evening the head hurts.

Research points the same way. In experiments by Rubinstein, Meyer and Evans, switching between tasks cost time, and the cost grew when the tasks were more complex or less familiar (APA). You may have seen the figure “up to 40% of productive time”: that is Meyer’s own estimate, not a result of the experiments. Sophie Leroy described attention residue: after a switch, part of our attention stays with the previous task (Leroy). So when you fly between continents, part of your luggage stays behind.

Yes, some people have always lived like this. Entrepreneurs, for example. But it is a small group, and it is hard for them too.

The second reason is social. If agents do the work, why wait a week? Stakeholders now expect a result after lunch, in an hour, at worst by the evening. Before, you had a week to sit and think. Now there is a rush, pressure, and a constant “faster, faster”.

The expectations are measurable. In a 2024 Upwork Research Institute survey, 96% of executives expected AI to raise productivity, while 77% of employees who used AI said it had added to their workload (Workplace Intelligence). Upwork sells freelance work, so take it with a grain of salt. The direction still matches what I see.

We do it to ourselves too. Agents are fast, so we want everything done now: skip the break, skip lunch, stay until night. We do less of the work with our own hands and sit at the computer longer. Anthropic’s engineers estimated that 27% of their work with Claude would not have been done at all without it (Anthropic). That is not saved time. That is new work.

Put this together, and you get a new belief: if an agent can jump between domains, a person can too, so you can load into a person’s head as much as you like. Is that true? No.

Nobody used to ask one developer, on one day, to add a button, write a marketing plan, go to the bank and discuss the business with stakeholders. Everyone knew it was too much. Now it is called a normal day.

Here the agent gives us the best analogy. When an agent’s context fills up, it starts to lose track of earlier instructions. Claude Code then compacts the conversation, and if you don’t say what to keep, something valuable can disappear. That is why you can write /compact focus on the auth bug fix. And an automatic compaction in the middle of a task comes at the worst possible moment (when to compact).

People don’t have a /compact command. Our compaction happens when we rest: when we sleep, walk, meditate, do something with our hands. Sleep is the big one. In deep sleep, slow waves of cerebrospinal fluid wash through the brain; researchers saw it in sleeping people with fast MRI in 2019 (Fultz and colleagues, Science). One sleepless night raised beta-amyloid, a protein linked to Alzheimer’s disease, by about 5% in the brains of 20 healthy people (NIH). And while we sleep, the brain is busy sorting what we learned during the day and fixing it in memory, as Diekelmann and Born summarized in their 2010 review. Even ten minutes of quiet rest with closed eyes after learning something helped people remember it a week later, in a small study of older adults (Dewar and colleagues, 2012).

If nobody gives you that time, the window overflows, and you stop taking in information, just like an agent with a full context. The human version of an auto-compact in the middle of a task is called staring at the wall after lunch.

Before, a man cut down a big baobab with an axe in half a day. Now he has a chainsaw and does it in 30 minutes. That doesn’t mean he should spend eight hours running around and cutting down 101 baobabs.

Some things will get faster. The economy will adjust, and the standards will change. But a person is still a person. That is the important part. People who studied, created or worked hard all day got headaches long before AI, and they used techniques that protect mental energy.

New techniques for the agent era haven’t been invented yet, and I’m not sure they need to be. The old ones still work, because the person hasn’t changed.

Focus blocks and real breaks. Pomodoro is decades old and still the simplest way to alternate effort and recovery. With agents, 25/5 and 50/10 both work; what matters is that the break is a break (Pomodoro with AI coding agents).

One domain per block. Code in one block, marketing in the next. Fewer continents per hour means fewer expensive trips.

Rest that holds your attention gently. A wandering mind is not a resting one: in a study of 2,250 people, minds wandered almost half of waking time, and people were less happy while it happened (Harvard Gazette). A walk in a park restored attention better than a walk down busy streets (APS). In a small study, experienced meditators’ minds wandered less (PubMed). Scrolling a feed is not on this list.

Sleep. It is the only full compaction we have.

Honest deadlines. Agents are fast; review, decisions, and people are not. Say it out loud when you agree on a deadline.

There is a small chance that you push through and achieve something big this way. There is a bigger chance that you burn out and give up. Neither is a plan. We have to learn to live and work with agents for years, not for one sprint.

So try an experiment. Take a real break. Come back and look at what happened while you were away. I promise nobody died in the meantime, and at the end of the day you will feel less tired.

The tools got faster; you don’t have to. Take one real break tomorrow and tell me what happened.

The Rise of AI Agents and What It Means for Workflow Automation
