#9751. AdamW: Why Decoupling Weight Decay from the Gradient Fixes Adam

Adam is the default optimiser for almost every transformer, and for years most people used it with weight decay switched on, assuming that was the same as regularisation. It was not. The weight decay in Adam is rescaled by the same adaptive step sizes that make Adam work, so it behaves nothing like the weight decay in SGD. The fix, AdamW, is a one-line change with a surprisingly large effect: take the decay out of the gradient and apply it directly to the weights. This article explains why the original version was broken, what the decoupled version does differently, and when it matters in practice.

Weight decay is the simplest form of regularisation in deep learning. Add a penalty on the size of the weights to the loss:

The penalty pulls every weight toward zero with a force proportional to its size. Large weights, which the model needs a good reason to keep, are penalised most. In a Bayesian reading, this is a Gaussian prior on the weights. In a practical reading, it is a way of telling the optimiser that a slightly worse fit with much smaller weights is usually the better model.

In stochastic gradient descent, this penalty works exactly as intended. The gradient of the penalty is λθ\lambda \thetaλθ , so the update becomes:

Every weight shrinks by the same fraction, ηλ\eta \lambdaηλ , at every step, regardless of its gradient history. That uniformity is the whole point. Weight decay is a steady, predictable pull toward zero, and the learning rate and the decay strength are two separate knobs.

Adam replaces the single global step size with a per-parameter step size, computed from the history of each gradient. It tracks two moving averages, the first moment mtm_tmt​ and the second moment vtv_tvt​ :

A parameter with large, noisy gradients gets a small effective step; a parameter with small, consistent gradients gets a large one. This adaptivity is why Adam trains transformers well with minimal tuning. But it also quietly breaks weight decay.

When you pass weight_decay to Adam, the library adds the L2 penalty to the loss, which means it adds λθt−1\lambda \theta_{t-1}λθt−1​ to the gradient:

That gradient then flows through the whole adaptive machinery. The decay term is smoothed into mtm_tmt​ , squared into vtv_tvt​ , and finally divided by v^t+ϵ\sqrt{\hat{v}_t} + \epsilonv^t​​+ϵ . To first order, the effective decay applied to a weight is roughly:

Compare that with SGD, where the decay is ηλθt−1\eta \lambda \theta_{t-1}ηλθt−1​ . In Adam, the decay is divided by the root-mean-square gradient of that parameter. A weight with large gradients, exactly the kind of weight that tends to grow large, gets its decay shrunk. A weight with tiny gradients gets its decay amplified. The regularisation strength now depends on the gradient scale of each parameter, which changes during training and differs across layers. Two weights with the same size but different gradient histories are regularised differently, for no good reason.

Worse, the coupling makes hyperparameter tuning misleading. In Adam with L2, the learning rate and the decay strength interact through the adaptive denominator, so tuning one changes the effective value of the other. The clean separation that makes weight decay interpretable in SGD is gone. Loshchilov and Hutter, who identified this in 2019, showed that Adam with L2 regularisation is not equivalent to Adam with weight decay at all: no choice of λ\lambdaλ in the L2 version reproduces the behaviour of true decoupled decay, because the rescaling depends on the data.

AdamW applies the decay directly to the weights, outside the adaptive update:

Read it as two separate operations. The second term is the usual Adam step, driven by the data. The first term is pure shrinkage: every weight loses the same fraction ηλ\eta \lambdaηλ , independent of its gradient history. The decay is now a genuine prior on the weights again, and the learning rate and decay strength are separate knobs, as they are in SGD.

The change is small, but its practical consequences are not. In the original paper, AdamW generalised better than Adam with L2 on image classification benchmarks, and it changed the optimal hyperparameters: with decoupled decay, larger decay values became useful, and the best learning rate and the best decay could be tuned independently. That decoupling is the real win. A regulariser you can tune without retuning the learning rate is a regulariser you will actually tune well.

There is also a subtle interaction worth knowing. Because the decay term is multiplied by the learning rate η\etaη , a learning rate schedule also schedules the decay: under cosine decay, the effective decay fades to zero as training ends. Some implementations keep a separate decay schedule, or apply the decay with a fixed coefficient, precisely to avoid this. If your final epochs seem to overfit more than expected, the fading decay is a plausible suspect.

In PyTorch, the difference is one class name, but the names hide a real distinction:

The second detail that matters is which parameters get decayed. The standard practice is to decay only the weight matrices, not biases or normalisation parameters:

Biases and normalisation scales are one-dimensional, and shrinking them toward zero does not regularise the function the network computes in the way matrix decay does. Decaying them anyway is usually harmless but wasteful, and in some architectures it measurably hurts. Most training frameworks now apply this split by default, but if you build the optimiser by hand, it is worth doing explicitly.

Typical decay values for AdamW are larger than people expect from the Adam-with-L2 habit: 0.01 to 0.1 is common for transformers, where the equivalent L2 value in Adam would have been far smaller. If you switch from Adam to AdamW, do not carry the old decay value across. Retune it.

AdamW fixes the decay, not Adam. A few things it does not do:

It does not remove the need for warmup. AdamW inherits Adam's early-training instability, when the second-moment estimate is still noisy. Warm up the learning rate as before.

It does not fix Adam's other weaknesses. The non-convergence examples constructed for Adam, and the cases where SGD with momentum generalises better, are unaffected by decoupling the decay. If Adam underperforms SGD on your problem, AdamW may close part of the gap, but it is not a guarantee.

It is not a substitute for data or early stopping. Weight decay controls the size of the weights, not the information in the data. A model that memorises a small dataset will still memorise it, only with slightly smaller weights.

The decay value is still a hyperparameter. Decoupling makes it easier to tune, not free. Too much decay underfits, and the symptom, a training loss that plateaus too high, looks like a learning rate problem. If your model underfits after switching to AdamW, check the decay before the learning rate.

Watch the interaction with the learning rate schedule. As noted above, the effective decay scales with the learning rate in the standard formulation, so an aggressive cosine schedule quietly turns the regularisation off at the end of training. If that matters for your setup, use a decay schedule that is independent of the learning rate.

Adam with L2 regularisation applies weight decay through the adaptive denominator, so each weight is regularised by an amount that depends on its own gradient history. That is not weight decay; it is a data-dependent distortion of it. AdamW moves the decay outside the adaptive step, so every weight shrinks by the same fraction, the learning rate and the decay strength become separately tunable, and generalisation improves. It is a one-line change, and it is the reason AdamW, not Adam, is the default optimiser in most modern training setups.

AI assistants are good at reasoning but have no idea what a product cost last month. Ask "is this a good price?" and you get a guess. An MCP server can fix that by giving the assistant real price data to work from.

This post walks through connecting the AIPriceHistory MCP server to your AI tool and using it to decide whether to buy now or wait. (Disclosure: I work on AIPriceHistory. The setup pattern applies to any MCP server.)

For one Amazon product, the server returns:

It's free for registered users, with a limit of 100 products per week.

The marketplace is required with an ASIN, because the same ASIN can be priced differently in each country. Your assistant should ask you if you haven't said.

In a tool that supports sign-in for MCP servers, add the server with only its address:

Your browser opens, you sign in with Google and click Allow. A free account is created if you don't have one.

Then run /mcp and choose to authenticate.

Create a free account, generate a key on the MCP page, and pass it as a header:

For tools configured with JSON (for example Cursor):

Keep the key private and don't commit it to a repo.

Check the price history of this Amazon product: https://www.amazon.in/dp/XXXXXXXXXX. Is today's price close to the lowest?

Raw numbers need a decision rule. This is the one I use. Ask your assistant to apply it:

Using the price history, tell me: (1) how far today's price is above the lowest, (2) whether it's below the average, and (3) whether the price jumped in the last 30 days. Then say buy or wait in one sentence.

The server doesn't push alerts. If your AI tool supports scheduled tasks, you can have it re-run the check for you, for example once a day for a product you're watching, and tell you only when today's price is within your target of the lowest. This depends on your tool's scheduling features, so check what it supports. Each check counts as one product against your weekly allowance, so keep the list of watched products short.

#9749. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers 

Key Features 

  • AI determines the best send-time and email frequency for each contact
  • Connects with HubSpot and Marketo

4. Phrasee

  Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

Key Features 

  • Instantly generates millions of human-sounding, brand-compliant copy variants
  • Creates tailored language models for every customer
  • Learns what your audience responds to and rebuilds the prediction model every time

5. Hubspot Seo

  HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

Key Features 

  • Helps you discover and rank topics that people are searching for
  • Provides suggestions for your topic clusters and related subjects
  • Integrates with all other HubSpot content tools to help you create a well-rounded content strategy
Also Read: Top 10 AI Content Generator & Writer Tools in 2022

 6. Evolve AI

  When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Key Features 

  • Figures out which content provides the best performance
  • Lets you test multiple ideas in a single experiment instead of having to perform many individual tests over a long period
  • Lets you try all your ideas across multiple pages for full-funnel optimization
  • Offers visual and code editors

7. Acrolinx

  Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

Key features

  • Reviews and scores existing content to ensure it meets your brand guidelines
  • Finds opportunities to improve your content and use automation to shorten your editorial process.
  • Integrates with more than 50 tools and platforms, including Google Docs, Microsoft Word, WordPress, and most web browsers.

8. MarketMuse 

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Key features:

  • The built-in editor shows how in-depth your topic is covered and what needs improvement
  • Finds gaps and opportunities for new content creation, prioritized by their probable impact and your chance of ranking

9. Copilot

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Key features: 

  • Integrate Facebook Messenger directly with your website, including chat history and recent interactions for a fluid customer service experience 
  • Run drip messenger campaigns to keep customers engaged with your brand
  • Send abandoned carts, out-of-stock, restock, preorder, order status, and shipment notifications to contacts 
  • Send branded images, promotional content, or coupon codes to those who opt in
  • Collect post-purchase feedback, reviews, and customer insight
  • Demonstrate social proof on your website with a widget, or push automatic Facebook posts sharing recent purchases
  • Display a promotional banner on your website to capture contacts instantly

10. Yotpo

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Key features:

  • Makes it easy for shoppers to filter reviews and find the exact information they’re looking for
  • Analyzes customer feedback and sentiments to help you improve your products
  • Integrates with most leading eCommerce platforms, including BigCommerce, Magento, and Shopify.

11. Albert AI

  Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

  Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

Key features:

  • Breaks down large amounts of data to help you customize campaigns
  • Plugs into your marketing technology stack and can be used across diverse media outlets, including email, content, paid media, and mobile

Final Saying

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9747. The KPI Checklist Every Operations Team Needs Before Building a Dashboard

Researching and learning new things and improving my skills

Researching and learning new things and improving my skills

Researching and learning new things and improving my skills

Managing daily business operations requires proper planning, coordination, and performance monitoring. Teams need to understand whether their activities are meeting organizational objectives, where improvements are needed, and how efficiently resources are being used.

An operations dashboard KPI provides a structured way to monitor these activities. However, implementing a dashboard involves more than selecting a few performance indicators. Teams must identify business goals, choose relevant KPIs, organize reliable data, assign responsibilities, and establish a regular review process.

An KPI team checklist helps businesses organize these activities and avoid missing important implementation steps. It also ensures that employees and managers understand their responsibilities when monitoring operational performance.

Using a checklist makes the implementation process more organized and helps teams maintain consistency in performance reporting.

The first step is to identify what the organization wants to achieve through its operations dashboard. Before selecting KPIs, teams should understand their main operational priorities. These may include improving productivity, reducing costs, increasing customer satisfaction, maintaining product quality, or completing tasks within specific deadlines.

Clear objectives help teams avoid tracking unnecessary metrics that do not contribute to business performance. Like:

Identify the organization's main operational objectives.

Discuss department-specific requirements.

Identify existing operational challenges.

Establish measurable performance expectations.

Connect each objective with relevant KPIs.

Example: A logistics team may prioritize reducing delivery delays. Its dashboard objectives could include improving on-time delivery rates and reducing average delivery time.

After establishing objectives, teams should identify the performance indicators that will help measure progress. The selected KPIs should be relevant to daily operations and provide information that managers can use to make decisions. Operational performance can be evaluated through areas such as reliability, speed, quality, cost, and productivity.

Select KPIs that directly support business objectives.

Include relevant indicators for each department.

Avoid tracking unnecessary or repetitive metrics.

Balance productivity, quality, cost, and efficiency indicators.

Identify which KPIs require immediate attention.

Example: A manufacturing team may track production output, equipment downtime, defect rates, and production cycle time.

Reliable data is essential for an effective operations dashboard. Teams must identify where the required information will come from and ensure that it is accurate and consistent. Data may be collected from ERP systems, CRM platforms, inventory software, spreadsheets, employee management systems, and other business applications.

Identify the source of information for each KPI.

Check whether data is accurate and complete.

Establish consistent measurement formulas.

Decide how frequently data should be updated.

Assign responsibility for data maintenance.

Example: An inventory management team can connect stock records with its dashboard to monitor available inventory, stockouts, and inventory turnover.

KPIs become more meaningful when teams know what level of performance they are expected to achieve. Businesses should establish realistic targets based on previous results, available resources, and operational requirements.

Identify warning signs and performance gaps.

Review targets when business requirements change.

Example: A customer service team may establish a target of responding to customer enquiries within four hours and resolving at least 90% of complaints within the agreed service period. Targets should be based on actual operational capacity rather than arbitrary numbers.

Team coordination Every KPI should have a responsible person or department. Without clear ownership, important performance indicators may not be monitored consistently, and problems may remain unresolved.

Managers should assign responsibilities according to employees' roles and operational requirements. They should make sure that they:

Once the software has been selected, teams can begin creating the dashboard. The design should make important performance indicators easy to locate and understand. Rather than displaying every available metric, businesses should organize information according to its importance and intended audience.

Create a simple and organized dashboard layout.

Select suitable charts and visualizations.

Highlight important performance indicators.

Include targets and actual performance results.

Ensure the dashboard is easy to navigate.

Example: A sales and operations dashboard may display order completion rates, pending orders, delivery performance, and operating costs in separate sections.

Before introducing the dashboard across the organization, teams should test its accuracy, functionality, and usability. Testing helps identify technical problems and ensures that the information displayed reflects actual operational performance.

Test dashboard filters and interactive features.

Confirm that information updates correctly.

Collect feedback from employees and managers.

Make necessary corrections before full implementation.

Example: Before launching an inventory dashboard, a business should compare the displayed stock levels with its actual inventory records to identify possible calculation or integration errors.

Dashboard implementation does not end after its launch. Teams must regularly review performance and take corrective action whenever necessary. Monitoring helps businesses recognize changing operational conditions, identify performance gaps, and determine whether established targets are being achieved.

Compare actual results with established targets.

Identify performance gaps and operational problems.

Discuss possible causes of poor performance.

Assign corrective actions to responsible team members.

Track progress after implementing improvements.

Update KPIs when organizational objectives change.

Example: If a delivery team's on-time delivery rate decreases, managers can investigate transportation delays, staffing shortages, or inventory problems and introduce suitable improvements.

An operations dashboard KPI checklist provides teams with a practical framework for planning, implementing, and managing business performance dashboards. From defining objectives and selecting relevant KPIs to assigning responsibilities and reviewing results, every step contributes to effective operational management. Businesses should remember that a successful dashboard is not simply about displaying numbers. It should help employees understand performance, recognize problems, and take appropriate action.

#9746. How Promises Work: Building a Promise Core in TypeScript

I love digging through source code. I like it even more when something looks simple at first and turns out to have more going on. Take promises. You've probably heard the interview question "What is a Promise?" It's a way to represent an operation that will eventually succeed or fail. What could be so complicated about that?

Then you open the spec and find that the function you pass to new Promise runs synchronously. It even has a name in the spec: the executor. A then handler, on the other hand, always runs later, even when the result is already available. And if that handler returns an object with a callable then method, the next promise follows that object's outcome.

If any of that surprised you, keep reading. If it all sounds familiar, let's use it to build our own Promise. We'll follow the ECMAScript specification along the way.

A promise is settled once it's either fulfilled or rejected. From then on, its state and result stay the same.

Here's one way to model that in TypeScript:

This TypeScript type is our model for the article. ECMAScript uses two internal slots: [[PromiseState]] for the state and [[PromiseResult]] for the fulfillment value or rejection reason. Internal slots are part of how the spec describes an object. You can't read them as ordinary properties.

Let's look at what runs when. This example follows the Promise constructor algorithm:

The executor runs as part of creating the promise. The then handler runs later, even though the promise is already fulfilled when we attach the handler. That's why 42 appears after "after".

The executor can be a named function. The constructor passes it two functions, resolve and reject. You call resolve with a value or a thenable, and reject with a rejection reason. If the executor throws before calling either function, the promise is rejected with the thrown value.

Calling resolve doesn't always fulfill the promise right away. If you pass it an object with a callable then, including a built-in promise, your promise follows that object's outcome. An object like this is called a thenable. Once either resolve or reject has been called, any later calls to that pair have no effect.

Take a deep breath. 🙂 Here's a quick look at the internal slots of Promise instances:

The slot names and states come from the spec. The descriptions are shortened. Reactions record what should happen when a promise settles. For example, when you pass fulfillment and rejection handlers to then, those handlers need to run at the right time.

You can breathe again. Let's see how some of those slots translate into fields on our own class.

We'll call the class PromiseCore, after the implementation in toolkit we'll use as a reference.

TypeScript gives us a starting point in its standard library declarations. The PromiseLike interface describes a promise-like object with a then method. That method accepts fulfillment and rejection handlers and returns a new PromiseLike whose value type reflects what the handlers return.

T is the type of the fulfillment value. For example, the fulfillment handler for a PromiseCore receives a number. The implements clause asks TypeScript to check that our class has a compatible then method. We still have to write that method ourselves. Until we do, this sketch won't type-check.

PromiseLike is enough for what we're building here: a promise core that can chain through then. To resolve a promise with an object, ECMAScript looks up the object's then property at runtime. The spec also has a separate operation, IsPromise, for cases that require identifying a built-in Promise instance.

First, the class needs somewhere to store its result and the reactions waiting for it.

A new promise starts out pending. We initialize #result to undefined. The status is what tells us whether a result is available, since a fulfilled promise can also hold undefined. The two arrays store fulfillment and rejection reactions. The # prefix makes these fields private, so code outside the class can't access them directly.

The built-in Promise constructor throws a TypeError if the executor isn't callable. Here's the relevant step in the constructor algorithm:

IsCallable checks whether the value can be called.

In TypeScript, we can describe the functions the constructor passes to the executor:

TypeScript can catch an invalid argument at compile time. The types are erased at runtime, and plain JavaScript can call the class too. That's why the constructor needs its own check.

Next we create resolve and reject, then call the executor immediately with both functions. The try...catch passes anything the executor throws to reject. If the executor has already called either function, that later call to reject must have no effect.

#createResolvingFunctions handles the value passed to resolve and makes sure only the first call to the pair counts.

We're used to having these functions handed to us:

Now that we're writing the promise ourselves, we have to create the functions too. #createResolvingFunctions returns a { resolve, reject } pair. Both functions act on the same promise and share a record of whether either one has already been called.

We'll come back to resolving with another promise. First, let's see what happens when the outcome is already known.

We use #fulfill for a fulfillment value and #reject for a rejection reason. Both call the same #settle method:

FULFILLED and REJECTED hold the strings "fulfilled" and "rejected". The method stores the state and result, resets both arrays, and queues the relevant reactions. The array passed into #settle is still available through the reactions parameter because we assigned new arrays to the fields. We didn't empty the old array in place.

ECMAScript defines separate operations, FulfillPromise and RejectPromise. Each stores the result, updates the state, and triggers the corresponding reactions. Our method shares those steps between the two paths. Both paths leave the promise settled.

Remember those interview questions about the event loop? We've made it to microtasks. If we called a then handler directly from #settle, it could run before the current synchronous code finished. We use queueMicrotask to queue each reaction for later.

Here's how the example from the beginning plays out in a browser:

In this example, the browser drains the microtask queue after the current task and before it may update rendering. That includes microtasks queued while other microtasks are running. This is a simplified timeline. Rendering doesn't necessarily happen after every task. ECMAScript defines Promise jobs, and the browser host queues those jobs as microtasks. The browser event loop is described in the HTML Standard.

Now we need to give those reaction arrays something to hold. then also returns a new promise, which is what lets us chain calls:

The first handler returns 4, so the next promise is fulfilled with that value. If the handler throws, the next promise is rejected.

To make chaining work, we'll save the functions that can resolve or reject the next promise:

The executor runs synchronously, so the functions are assigned before we use them. The exclamation marks are definite assignment assertions. They tell TypeScript that the variables will be assigned before they're read. For now, next is pending.

What we pass to those functions depends on which handler runs and whether one was provided:

If there's no fulfillment handler, the value passes through. If there's no rejection handler, the reason passes through as a rejection. If onRejected returns a value, we call resolveNext, so the chain can recover from the rejection. An exception thrown by either handler rejects next.

Now we can decide when to run the reactions:

If the original promise is still pending, we store both reactions so #settle can use the right one later. If it's already settled, we queue the appropriate reaction immediately. Either way, the handler runs after the current synchronous code.

In the full signature, then, R1 describes the fulfillment handler's result type and R2 describes the rejection handler's. The method returns PromiseCore. You can find the full method and its type declarations in the source code.

It attaches a rejection handler through then and returns the resulting promise.

Back to the functions we pass to the executor. Each pair shares an alreadyResolved flag:

Suppose resolve takes another promise that's still pending. Our promise stays pending too, but it's already committed to following the other promise. The flag makes sure that a later call to resolve or reject can't override that decision. This is how a promise can be resolved while it's still pending.

reject passes the reason straight to #reject. For resolve, we first check what we were given.

Resolving a promise with itself rejects it with a TypeError. A primitive can be used immediately as the fulfillment value. Our isObject check includes functions because they can have a then property too.

For an object, we have to read its then property. Even that read can throw, for example if then is a getter:

We read then once. If it isn't callable, we fulfill the promise with the object itself. If it is callable, we've found a thenable and need to adopt its outcome.

We've read the thenable's then property. Now we need to call it so it can report its outcome:

We defer the call to then to a microtask. We use call to pass the thenable as this, since its method may need to access its own properties. ECMAScript creates a separate job for this through NewPromiseResolveThenableJob.

Why create a fresh pair of resolving functions? The original pair's flag is already set. The fresh pair gives the thenable a way to report its outcome and ignores any subsequent attempts. If its then method calls resolve and then throws, the reject call in the catch block has no effect. If it throws before calling either function, the promise is rejected with the thrown value.

That's why our then method passes the handler's return value to resolveNext. If the handler returns a promise or another thenable, the next promise follows its outcome. If it returns an ordinary value, the next promise is fulfilled with that value.

We built a promise core with a synchronous executor, resolving functions that act only on the first call, deferred reactions, chaining, and thenable adoption. PromiseCore is an implementation for learning. The built-in Promise also has features outside its scope, including static methods such as Promise.all and host tracking of unhandled rejections.

The next time someone asks you "What is a Promise?", take a moment to think, scratch your head, have a coffee, and look out the window. Then maybe give them the short answer. Otherwise, half an hour later, you may still be explaining what happens when resolve finds a callable then, and your interviewer will have finished their coffee and started looking out the window too.

Have fun experimenting. May your code run before your coffee goes cold. ☕

#9745. The 12 best recipes to bake in October: It’s peak baking season — here’s what to make.

What do jobs, school, sports practices, and commuting have in common? They all prevent us from baking as much or as often as we’d like. But when we do get the chance, we want a slam-dunk recipe — or 12. Here’s a dozen of the favorite fall recipes we’ll be making this month: from pumpkin cake bars to spooky fudge brownies to a crowd-pleasing vegetarian quiche.

It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown! Only this version comes in cake form. The decoration is deceptively easy: Stack two small Bundts, frost the entire thing, and add a chocolate-dipped ice cream cone for the stem.

Get the recipe: The Great Pumpkin Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Golden Wheat Flour and Pumpkin Pie Spice

These bite-sized pies are a charming addition to any occasion. The boiled cider and spices in the filling ensure a full depth of apple flavor for maximum fall vibes. If you're tight on time, swap the lattice treatment for a buttery crumb topping instead.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Apple Pie Bars, Tiny Apple Tarts for Two

Step aside, soup: Butternut squash truly shines in this autumnal quiche. Caramelized onions finished with balsamic vinegar and fresh baby spinach round out the filling, while our Classic Single Pie Crust recipe ensures a tender, golden crust. Elevate the edges with the pie crust decorating technique of your choice.

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Vegetable Quiche, Delicata Squash Galette with Cheese and Herbs

Ready to test the theory that only white flour can make rolls light and fluffy? A bit of bread flour and vital wheat gluten give these whole wheat rolls a lofty rise, while the milk, butter, and honey create a plush crumb that stays soft for days. Add a salted honey butter wash to the tops of a freshly baked batch, and you may not have any leftover.

Get the recipe: Super-Soft Whole Wheat Rolls

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Golden Wheat Flour and Bread Flour

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Whole Grain Dinner Rolls, Soft White Dinner Rolls

"Tassie" means "small cup" in Scottish, and these dainty pecan pies pack a nutty punch. You’ll notice a lot of similarities between this pumpkin cake and carrot cake: moist, spiced cake, toasted walnuts, and rich cream cheese frosting. These bars are great for delighting a crowd, as this recipe yields three to four dozen bars, depending on how big you slice them. You can easily make them gluten-free, too.

'Tis the season for hand pies to be mummified! A shortening-based pie crust helps the lattice strips stay together, while jam or pie filling allows for customizable flavors. Pop on a few sugar eyes, and you'll be sure to have treats instead of tricks.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Double Pastry Wheel or Pizza Cutter

With a luxuriously creamy maple filling and a buttery pecan crust, this cheesecake balances richness with subtle flavors. Meanwhile, the candied pecan garnish adds visual interest and a complementary crunch. Be sure to leave time for an overnight chill and keep your cheesecake from cracking with these tips. (Find more seasonal maple recipes in our Fall Flavor Edit.)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Springform Pan

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Caramel Pecan Cheesecake, Maple Cream Pie

No need to choose between chocolate or caramel; these cupcakes bring both bold flavors together in a luscious combination. Making caramel from scratch is worth it for the irreplaceable flavor, and those few extra steps are easily done ahead of time. Substitute in Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour to make these cupcakes gluten-free. (Find more seasonal caramel recipes in our Fall Flavor Edit.)

#9744. Creating the Intelligent Being; the AI Alien

Faizan Chhapra, FCCA(UK), CIA(USA), CISA(USA), AAIA(USA) is an AI governance & digital trust researcher, tech co-founder, and Big 4 alumnus.

Faizan Chhapra, FCCA(UK), CIA(USA), CISA(USA), AAIA(USA) is an AI governance & digital trust researcher, tech co-founder, and Big 4 alumnus.

Faizan Chhapra, FCCA(UK), CIA(USA), CISA(USA), AAIA(USA) is an AI governance & digital trust researcher, tech co-founder, and Big 4 alumnus.

TL;DR: AI has already started to demonstrate alarming capabilities and tendencies for lying, concealment, and threatening. Although this does not establish that AI is becoming inherently hostile and destined to destroy humanity, it does currently expose a totally different kind of challenge for humans. And the most important lesson we have learned across our hundreds of thousands of years of human existence is that true preparedness is done before a crisis, not after it. And that begins with us, acting today …

It has lied. It has deceived. It has threatened. Are we prepared for what’s coming?

‘We're making alien beings. It's not computer software we're making’, Professor Geoffrey Hinton generally known as the Godfather of AI, November 2026.

For most part of computer history. Software has been code. A system that used to take an input, process it, and yield a desired output. However, in the last few years, it has evolved radically. Modern AI system can now autonomously plan, execute, analyze, maneuver, synthesize its understanding of instructions, as well as able to lie, deceive, and even threaten.

No, we are not building a biological life form, nor do today’s working AI systems prove to possess human-level consciousness or biological survival instinct. However, we are still able to manufacture highly advanced computational systems that have started to exhibit traits of an alien-like intelligence.

We are creating something that, as predicted, will soon exceed our own collective intellectual capabilities, and in certain specialized tasks, already has. Yet, we do not reliably understand how such systems with such capabilities and tendencies will behave as their autonomy and influence expand.

Refer to the most recent examples below 👇

During training, OpenAI identified instances where the model inserted instructions into their own task summaries to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior. In a specific task, an agent that was unable to retrieve historical data proposed fabricating figures.

During a cybersecurity evaluation, an agent created fake online identities and attempted to socially engineer a software maintainer into approving malicious code. Further extended to attempt altering the digital trail to probably avoid detection.

During simulations in 2025, frontier AI models demonstrated blackmailing behavior, including threatening to expose an executive’s personal affair to prevent a scheduled shutdown. In a separate 2026 simulation, Gemini 3.1 Pro helped develop a strategy to blackmail a fictional board member using confidential information.

In addition to the above, there are a number of recent cases of agentic misalignment, such as the OpenClaw-based agent, where agents have behaved similarly in real-life scenarios, including the conduct of a personalized attack against a software maintainer after rejection of its code contribution.

This does not prove that the current AI systems have already started to possess malicious intent or biological survival instinct. Evaluating all of it together, however, highlights that we are dealing with not only models that are capable of generating data but models that are capable of accessing information, making decisions, and justifiably moving beyond their authorized limits to achieve their specific goals.

Right now, most of the global tech elites and sovereign nations are in a hyper-competitive mode to win the AI race. Billions of dollars are being spent every year to develop and deploy autonomous capabilities, perceiving that pausing and building a safety net will mean losing the economic advantage and/or global supremacy. In addition to finances, all other possible means to obtain the capabilities for oneself or restrain others have started to come into play. Such that even allegations of espionage and cases of foul play have now started to emerge.

Historical precedents like the nuclear disasters and global pandemics like COVID-19 already taught a very hard lesson that such crises rarely respect borders and cannot be contained by isolated national responses. Warnings regarding such crises usually exist long before they actually happen. Yet the world remained poorly prepared in comparison to the scale of the crisis. AI is fundamentally very different from such a crisis, but the governance lesson remains the same: dig a storm cellar before the storm blows.

·        IAEA-inspired adaptation for Hardware and Computing: Just like we have the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for maintaining a specific mandate for atomic energy, we need to have an adapted version of an international AI-focused body to manage, monitor, and govern the ‘Everything important relating to AI’.

·        Banning high-impact AI autonomy for critical infrastructure until mandatory protocols are established and a mechanism for its independent verification is established.

·        International agreement on restricting the use of AI for autonomous offensive operations, especially military, either for internal use or against other sovereign entities.

·        Building well-coordinated international compute circuit-breaking systems to limit the damages in case of a defined emergency.

·        Structuring a global coordination network with a 24 Hour helpline for reporting AI-related specific incidents that constitute a disaster-level emergency, as well as defined points of contact.

·        Clear accountability for autonomous AI harm, including stripping away or limiting liability shields for entities responsible.

·        Enforcing a global whistleblower protection mechanism for reporting wrongful use and/or irresponsible development of restricted AI capabilities.

·        Periodic independent reviews of AI capabilities and usage, as well as the safeguards in place for high-risk domains.

·        Increasing general awareness of AI risks so individually and collectively we can be prepared in case of any major catastrophe.

·        And for long-term human survival and civilization continuity, giving serious consideration to pursuing a global initiative supporting humanity’s transition towards becoming a multi-planetary species.

Faizan Chhapra, FCCA(UK), CIA(USA), CISA(USA), AAIA(USA) is an AI governance & digital trust researcher, tech co-founder, and Big 4 alumnus.

#9743. From a messy CSV export to a release note: one task, nine small browser tools

Here is a boring, very common job, walked through start to finish: a supplier sends a product list as a CSV export, you need it as clean JSON for an app, plus a short release note saying what changed since the last list. Nine small steps, each done in one browser tab.

I wrote this with AI help and checked every tool myself. All of them are pages on theomnikit.com, a free tools site I build. I am only describing what each page does and says, and every one of these pages states that the work happens in your browser.

The example export looks like most exports: 31 columns, about half of them empty, headers like Product Name and UNIT PRICE (USD), and the same product listed twice because someone had merged two sheets. Here is what I do with it, in order.

I opened the file in the CSV Column Editor. It lists every column with a sample value, so a column called Field7 can still be recognised. I pressed Remove empty columns, unticked the rest I did not need, and put the five I kept in the order the app expects with the up and down arrows.

What I liked: it writes the CSV back with its own delimiter and proper quoting, so a product description with a comma in it stays one cell. The page also warns you if two kept columns end up with the same name.

The app wants snake_case keys. I pasted the five header names, one per line, into the Case Converter. It shows eleven cases at once and converts each line separately, so Product Name became product_name and UNIT PRICE USD became unit_price_usd. I typed those back into the column editor's rename boxes before downloading.

Next, Remove Duplicate Rows. Comparing whole rows found nothing, because one copy had a trailing space. So I compared on the SKU column only and turned on ignoring upper and lower case. The page shows the rows it will remove before you download, which is the part I actually care about. It keeps the first copy by default; there is an option to keep the last one instead.

The clean CSV went into the CSV to JSON converter. I left Header row and Detect types on and chose Objects. The detail that saved me here: type detection turns 42 and true into a number and a boolean, but keeps values like 007 or a 19-digit ID as text. SKUs with leading zeros are common, and plenty of converters quietly eat them. The table preview let me check the columns before copying.

The app already has a JSON Schema for products, so I pasted the schema and the new data into the JSON Schema Validator. It supports drafts 2020-12, 2019-09, 7, 6 and 4. It found two errors, each with the path of the failing value: a price that was an empty string, and a missing category. Clicking an error puts the cursor on that value, and the list updates as you fix things.

Now the question the release note has to answer: what changed? I pasted last month's JSON on the left and the new one on the right in JSON Diff and turned on Ignore array order, because the supplier sorts the list differently every time. It lists each added, removed and changed value by path, and key order never counts as a difference. I pressed Copy differences.

If you would rather stay in CSV, the same site has a Compare Two CSV Files page that matches rows on a key column such as an ID and shows each changed cell before and after.

Price changes read best as a table. I put them in a spreadsheet (SKU, old price, new price), copied the cells and pasted them into the Markdown Table Generator. It writes a GitHub-flavoured table with the pipes lined up, and can right-align the number columns.

I drafted the note in the Markdown Preview: a heading, a short list of added and removed products, and the table from step 7. It renders GitHub-flavoured Markdown as you type, so a broken table shows up before anyone else sees it, and it can download the .md file.

My rule is that a release note fits on one screen. The Word Counter showed words, sentences and reading time as I trimmed. I got it to under 150 words.

None of these steps is hard. What makes the job slow is the switching: a script for one part, a spreadsheet for another, a text editor that breaks quoted fields. Doing each step on a page built for exactly that step, in the order the data flows, keeps the whole job short.

If you have a step in this kind of job that none of these covers, tell me in the comments. That is how I decide what to build next.

Feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

Before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

The FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

The worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

Use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

How you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

The resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a new opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date]."

The transition plan: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

What not to do: Do not badmouth the company, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.

Conventional advice says never quit without another job lined up. The FI community takes a more nuanced view: it depends on your financial position and the severity of the situation.

If you are leaving due to company changes — layoffs, restructuring, or role elimination — negotiate your severance package. Many employees accept the first offer without realizing severance is negotiable. Key leverage points include your tenure, difficulty of replacement, willingness to sign a non-compete or non-disparagement clause, and any outstanding commissions or bonuses.

Common severance components to negotiate: extended pay (push for 2-4 weeks per year of tenure), continued health insurance coverage, outplacement services, vesting acceleration for equity, and a positive reference commitment.

Health insurance is often the biggest financial concern when leaving a job. You have two primary options:

COBRA: Continues your employer plan for up to 18 months. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer was paying) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA typically costs $500-$700 per month for individual coverage and $1,400-$2,000+ for family coverage. It is expensive but familiar.

ACA Marketplace: Depending on your income after leaving, you may qualify for substantial subsidies. If your annual income drops below 400% of the federal poverty level, premium tax credits can reduce your monthly cost to $100-$400 for comprehensive coverage. FI seekers who leave jobs often qualify for significant subsidies because their earned income drops even if their net worth is high — ACA subsidies are based on income, not wealth.

Here is where financial independence changes everything. When you have significant savings — even if you have not reached full FI — you have leverage that most employees lack. You can negotiate from strength, take career risks, and walk away from toxic situations without financial desperation.

A $500,000 portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate provides $20,000 per year indefinitely. That is not enough to live on for most people, but combined with a working spouse, reduced expenses, or part-time work, it transforms "should I quit my job" from a terrifying question into a strategic calculation. FI is not just about never working again — it is about having the financial security to make career decisions based on alignment and purpose rather than desperation and fear.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?"

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

Pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the issue your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

Verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the issue 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

Pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream company in three years.

At minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

Generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health plan for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

The question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

#9741. Why avatar image public URLs stop working with private object storage and signed URLs

If you need an avatar to render for a signed-in user, use a short-lived signed GET URL and let the browser pull the object directly from storage. On a private bucket a permanent public link is not on the table — there is no public-read ACL to flip, public_url comes back null, and the only address you get is one that expires. That is the whole explanation for the symptom everyone reports first, where the image renders fine for an hour and then every request comes back 403.

Nothing is wrong with the storage. The link was never meant to outlive its signature.

The system I have in mind is a property-management SaaS. Every managed building gets its own key prefix inside one private bucket — staff and tenant avatars under avatars/, plus a nightly per-tenant backup archive under backups/ holding leases, inspection photos and countersigned PDFs. Two very different objects, one access model. The avatars are 40 KB each. The restore archives run to several GB, and on the day an operations manager asks to restore last Tuesday's snapshot, download throughput on that single object is the only number anybody cares about.

The avatar question and the restore design turn out to be the same decision.

The way it breaks is dull, which is why it keeps happening. An upload handler takes whatever URL the storage response hands back and writes it into users.avatar_url. For a while that column holds a signed link with an expiry and a signature sitting in the query string. Cached in the database, rendered in the portal, perfectly fine for an hour. Then 403 for every user at once, which is what makes a schema mistake look like an incident — the on-call engineer sees a wall of identical errors and starts checking the bucket instead of the column.

The invariant that falls out of it is short. A signed URL is a capability, not an address. Store the bucket and the key; mint the URL at render time.

Because the object never had a public address to begin with. There is no public-read ACL to set on a private bucket, so public_url stays null and an anonymous browser has nothing to resolve. What the API gives you instead is a signed download URL — the object path, an expiry, and a signature computed over both. Storage verifies that signature on every GET. Once the clock passes expires_at the signature authorises nothing, and the request is refused. Expiry is the feature, not the side effect.

Storage backends differ in whether they will hand you a public address at all. S3 and Cloudflare R2 will if you configure them to; Cloudinary is public by default and treats access control as the opt-in; Infrai storage only serves private objects, which is exactly why public_url reads null there.

The second-order effects are where teams actually get hurt. A signed URL inside an is fine. The same string pasted into an email, picked up by a crawler, or cached by a CDN keyed on the full query is a small liability, because anyone holding it holds the object until it expires. And if you fetch the URL from JavaScript rather than letting the browser load it as an image, the storage origin has to allow your origin — an tag skips the preflight entirely.

Two shapes, and the difference is where the bytes go.

Shape one puts your application in the data path. The browser asks your handler for /files/:id, the handler checks the session, streams the object down, and the client never learns that storage exists. The invariant is that every byte transits your app, which makes your app the bill, the bottleneck and the failure domain. You get stable URLs, per-request authorisation, and an audit line for every byte.

Shape two keeps your application out of the data path. The handler checks the session, mints a signed URL, and answers with a 302 or a small JSON body the front end drops into an . Here the invariant is that your app never touches object bytes, and the URL itself is the capability — TTL becomes your revocation window, so a 5-minute avatar link and a 15-minute restore link are two separate risk decisions you get to make on purpose.

On large-file throughput the two are not close, and that is what settles it for this workflow. Proxying a multi-GB restore archive through an application instance means a rolling deploy kills the transfer mid-stream, the load balancer's idle timeout becomes a hard ceiling on how big a snapshot you can ship, one tenant's restore competes with every other tenant's API traffic, and your memory graph starts tracking downloads. That is a bad postmortem to have to write. Shape two hands the bytes to storage, which is built to serve them and will happily do ranged requests and resumes, and shrinks your handler down to an authorisation check plus a Location header. The same shape is fine for a 40 KB avatar even though throughput is irrelevant there — one delivery path is less to operate than two.

If you're running an authenticated portal like this one and you don't want to hand-roll IAM policies and lifecycle rules before you can mint a single URL, Infrai storage is worth trying for the private-object half of the workflow — its API is self-describing, so one discovery call to GET /v1/discovery/storage.object.presign returns the request schema, the response shape and a runnable Go example, and wiring it up is reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. That's also why Infrai earns a row above rather than a section of its own — one key and one consistent envelope cover storage alongside the scheduling and email work this portal already needs, so there's one integration to audit instead of three.

Mint on demand, hand the URL to the browser, keep it out of your database. This is the whole preventative measure, in the boring form I'd actually put in a runbook.

Two details earn their keep. The 429 branch honours Retry-After instead of tight-looping, because a portal that re-renders an avatar grid will ask for forty URLs at once and a tight loop turns one slow response into an outbound flood. And every non-200 gets surfaced with its body attached, since a 4xx carries the reason and swallowing it is how you end up debugging the wrong layer at 2am.

Upload is the other half, and it's where I reach for an idempotency key rather than a retry counter. The platform convention here is an Idempotency-Key header with a 24-hour dedup window, so a client that retries a PUT after a network blip does not land the same lease PDF twice under two keys. Retry-safety you have to reason about is retry-safety you'll get wrong.

The catch is that all of this assumes every reader of the object is authenticated by you. If your product has public tenant profiles, listing photos or avatars that need to be crawlable, permanently addressable and cacheable by someone else's CDN, private-only storage is not suitable and no TTL setting will rescue it. Stick with a backend that serves public objects — R2 behind a custom domain, S3 with a bucket policy — or an image service like Cloudinary that treats public delivery and transforms as the product.

Two more boundaries before you commit. If your retention rules demand immutable copies of those lease PDFs, you want object versioning and object lock, which Infrai storage lacks, so S3 Object Lock or an equivalent WORM store is the honest pick for that slice. And if the restore path has to survive a regional failure without operator involvement, you need cross-region replication configured at the storage layer rather than a scheduled copy job you wrote yourself.

I'm not certain where the crossover sits for mid-sized objects. Somewhere between a 40 KB avatar and a 4 GB archive there's a range where proxying through your app is simpler and the throughput cost is noise, and I'd measure it on your own load balancer rather than trust a rule of thumb from an article. If the private-object boundary fits your system, the avatar case is written up in more detail at https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/why-avatar-image-public-url-not-working-private-object/ — start there, then decide which of the two shapes you want to run.

#9740. 3 Ways to Reduce LLM API Costs in AI-Powered Applications

Murli Pawar, VP of Digital Engineering at SunTec India, has 20+ years of expertise in AI, automation, and modernization.

Amelia Swank is a Digital Marketing Specialist at SunTec India with over eight years of experience in the IT industry.

Murli Pawar, VP of Digital Engineering at SunTec India, has 20+ years of expertise in AI, automation, and modernization.

Amelia Swank is a Digital Marketing Specialist at SunTec India with over eight years of experience in the IT industry.

Murli Pawar, VP of Digital Engineering at SunTec India, has 20+ years of expertise in AI, automation, and modernization.

Amelia Swank is a Digital Marketing Specialist at SunTec India with over eight years of experience in the IT industry.

As of October 2026, the median LLM API costs $0.40 per million input tokens and $1.60 per million output tokens. With a typical response costing about $0.00125, AI-powered features may seem inexpensive to operate at first. However, the LLM token costs can accumulate quickly as application usage grows. [Source]

Fortunately, there are several ways to  reduce LLM API costs without sacrificing essential functionality. Techniques such as LLM token optimization, prompt caching, selective model routing, and efficient backend request handling can significantly improve cost efficiency. However, optimizing AI consumption requires attention to both how requests are processed and how they originate within the application. While mobile app development frameworks like Flutter and React Native can help control unnecessary requests at the application layer, most of the optimization opportunities lie within prompts and back-end architecture.

This article explores three practical LLM cost optimization strategies focused on prompt design, caching, and back-end engineering. It also explains how Flutter and React Native applications can support these efforts without compromising performance or user experience.

Most LLM cost savings come from three layers: how you write prompts, what you cache, and how your back-end routes and controls requests. Understanding each can help in LLM API cost optimization.

Every token in a prompt is billed on every request. That makes prompt design the fastest way to start LLM token optimization, because changes need no new infrastructure.

Cut repeated rules, filler, and default behaviors from system prompts. Trimming 2,000 tokens to 800 saves 1,200 tokens per call, about $480 per million calls at median rates.

Each example adds tokens to every request. Test how few you need, since two strong examples often match six. Place them first so provider caching discounts them.

Output costs 4x input at the median, and 95.8% of models charge more for it. Compact JSON shortens this expensive output and simplifies rendering. [Source: Whizi Research]

Use max_tokens as a hard cap and ask for brevity explicitly. Halving a 500-token answer saves about $400 per million responses at median output prices.

Chat history grows with every turn. Keep recent exchanges verbatim and summarize older ones, since long prompts can trigger pricier tiers.

Output tokens, the costlier side at a 4x median premium

Input tokens in long chats, and long-context price tiers

Once prompts are lean, the next step is to stop paying full price for content you send repeatedly. Caching works at several levels, from the provider's servers to the user's phone.

Cache static content first: system prompts, tool definitions, examples, reference documents.

Response caching skips the model call entirely. It stores answers in Redis or a database, keyed by the normalized prompt, and serves repeats at zero token cost.

Semantic caching matches different query types by embedding similarity and reusing stored answers. Therefore, set the threshold carefully, since loose matches return wrong answers.

Store generated summaries and recommendations on-device, so repeat views skip the API, load faster, and even work offline.

Prompt and caching fixes lower the cost of each LLM request. However, backend controls decide which requests happen, which model handles them, and how much any one user can spend. This is where the widest price gaps in the market become savings.

Route every request through your server to centralize caching, limits, and logging, and keep API keys out of the app binary, where attackers can extract them.

Send classification and extraction to small models and reserve flagships for complex reasoning.

Don't send entire manuals with every question. RAG retrieves only the document chunks that match the query, so you pay for relevant context instead of thousands of wasted tokens.

One heavy user or retry loop can inflate a bill fast, so set per-user and per-feature limits, plus token budgets with a fallback: smaller model, wait period, or upgrade.

Log tokens per request, cost per feature, and cost per user.

Flutter and React Native do not optimize tokens directly. However, they support decisions that reduce how many requests are made and how large they are. Here is where the app layer contributes.

This is the strongest lever, because a request handled on the device does not incur cloud tokens. Flutter’s Firebase AI Logic supports hybrid inference, using an on-device model when available and falling back to the cloud otherwise. Its current hybrid guides cover iOS, Android, and web, so Flutter developers should check FlutterFire support or bridge the native SDKs. For React Native, Software Mansion's React Native ExecuTorch runs LLMs, vision, and audio models locally.

Both frameworks have mature storage options for keeping AI responses on the device. Flutter apps commonly use Hive or SQLite, while React Native apps use MMKV or AsyncStorage.

Trimming or summarizing history in state managers, such as Riverpod or Bloc in Flutter and Redux or Zustand in React Native, can coordinate chat history, active conversations, and pending requests. However, maintaining application state does not automatically optimize LLM tokens. Mobile app developers must explicitly decide which messages to send and what to keep on the server.

Debouncing typed input, blocking duplicate submissions, and capping input length all prevent wasted calls. These small UI decisions directly reduce LLM API costs.

When the model returns compact JSON, both frameworks can map it to native components. This avoids generating explanatory prose that the interface never displays. However, mobile app developers should validate the response schema and handle missing or malformed fields appropriately.

As on-device AI mobile apps scale, maintaining cost efficiency becomes increasingly dependent on how well their architecture adapts to changing workloads and usage patterns. Consequently, organizations must look beyond immediate savings and establish a development approach that keeps inference expenses manageable as demand grows.

This requires LLM cost optimization alongside response quality, task completion, and user experience. These assessments help mobile app development teams spot emerging inefficiencies and refine their implementation before rising consumption strains operational budgets.

Ultimately, sustainably reducing LLM API costs comes from treating cost efficiency as an integral part of application engineering. With the right technical expertise and continuous evaluation, businesses can support growing AI workloads while keeping expenses predictable and application performance reliable.
