#9738. "Connected" is not a diagnosis: three readings that are

"Connected" is the least useful status a network client can show. It means a tunnel exists. It does not mean traffic flows, and it does not mean the route is any good. Three readings get you further than the word itself.

If the status line shows a route and a latency figure, the tunnel is up and the client is talking to something. If it shows only "connected" with no number, the tunnel is not actually established — usually a permission prompt that was dismissed during the first run, or a firewall rule that never got added.

On Windows this is the virtual adapter permission. On macOS it is the network extension. On mobile it is the VPN configuration. Each is asked once, and each fails silently afterwards.

Absolute latency tracks physical distance, so a cross-continent route will always look worse than a city one. What matters is the spread:

Write down the time of each disconnect for thirty minutes.

Those three readings cover most of what "it keeps dropping" actually means. I keep a longer write-up with the four-layer order — local network, system power management, protocol or network restrictions, then route congestion — and the signal to look for at each layer here: QuickQ connection self-check

There is a separate page for the drop-specific diagnosis: four-layer drop triage

Both are part of an independent handbook, not vendor documentation. They document the readings and the next step, not a promise.

#9736. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

#9735. Europe's Supermarket Cyberattacks Expose a Bigger Problem With Connected Infrastructure

Associate Professor at University of Calabria. Researching LLMs, trustworthy AI, and data science. Writing on AI, tech, and society.

Associate Professor at University of Calabria. Researching LLMs, trustworthy AI, and data science. Writing on AI, tech, and society.

Associate Professor at University of Calabria. Researching LLMs, trustworthy AI, and data science. Writing on AI, tech, and society.

In recent weeks, many European supermarkets have discovered that a cyberattack can turn a refrigerator into a source of heat. Modern refrigeration systems use an automatic defrost cycle that periodically suspends cooling and heats certain components to remove ice from the coils, ensuring that the system operates properly. This process can also be controlled remotely. On the night of October 11–12, hundreds of French supermarkets were targeted by cyberattacks that manipulated refrigeration controls, extending defrost cycles and causing substantial food losses. At one Intermarché store in Gradignan, the owner reported that the temperature in a cold room had reached 50°C. On November 2, Reuters documented a new wave of incidents affecting supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, and other European countries, including another reported case of freezers reaching 50°C in Stockholm. Refrigeration incidents were also reported in Ireland, while Italian authorities confirmed that a limited number of stores had been affected.

In a previous article published on HackerNoon, titled Houston, We Have a Problem: Artificial Intelligence Is Becoming Harder to Control, we had already pointed to a particularly dangerous combination. Over the years, we have connected a growing number of systems to the Internet, often prioritizing convenience and cost savings over security. Controlling equipment remotely avoids costly on-site visits and allows for quick intervention, but it also exposes the system to potential attacks. This growing connectivity is not always matched by adequate security measures: some systems may run outdated software, use default passwords that have never been changed, rely on devices that manufacturers no longer update, or expose services directly to the Internet without sufficient safeguards. And hospitals, transportation, power grids, and other essential services now depend on these infrastructures. Meanwhile, we are developing increasingly powerful AI systems capable of writing code, using tools, and identifying vulnerabilities. So-called AI agent swarms are also emerging: groups of autonomous agents that divide tasks, work in parallel, share information, and adapt their strategies. If used maliciously, these technologies could enable attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities at speeds and on a scale that would have been unthinkable until recently. And this is where the paradox lies: as the tools for attacking grow ever more powerful, our society depends on increasingly complex digital infrastructures, often built up in a piecemeal fashion, tightly interconnected, and running software that may contain vulnerabilities.

The supermarket incidents bring an increasingly important question back into focus: if artificial intelligence is becoming such a powerful tool in the hands of attackers, why should it not be equally powerful for those defending against them? The answer lies in a fundamental feature of cybersecurity that AI may amplify: the asymmetry between attack and defense. An attacker may need to find just one vulnerability, while defenders must protect servers, applications, devices, and external connections all at once. Attackers can choose where and when to strike; defenders must be prepared for threats coming from anywhere in their infrastructure. Imagine what might happen if a hacker tasked a swarm of AI agents with autonomously exploring an infrastructure and identifying its weakest points. There is no evidence that autonomous AI agents played a role in the recent supermarket attacks, which illustrate the risks of insecure connectivity rather than AI-driven cyberattacks. The scenario is nevertheless worth considering because increasingly autonomous AI systems could make identifying and exploiting similar weaknesses faster and more scalable.

Using AI for defense, however, is far more complicated. An experiment published by Corma in August 2026 offers an interesting example. The company tested four frontier AI models in 241 attack-and-defense engagements within a controlled enterprise network. The attacking agents attempted to install persistent backdoors, while defending agents were subsequently tasked with identifying them. According to Corma, attackers established verified, reboot-surviving backdoors in 85% of engagements, whereas defenders correctly identified the planted artifacts in 22% of cases involving a verified persistent backdoor. These figures measure different outcomes and come from a specific experimental setup, rather than demonstrating a universal performance gap between offensive and defensive AI. Nevertheless, they highlight an important challenge: successfully exploiting a weakness and reliably detecting its exploitation are fundamentally different tasks.

Detecting an attack is not simply a matter of spotting unusual behavior: an authorized technician and a hacker who has stolen the technician’s credentials could issue identical commands. Moreover, attackers can afford numerous failed attempts, while defenders cannot keep shutting down essential services at every sign of suspicion. An AI system that mistakenly shut down a refrigeration unit could cause damage similar to what it was trying to prevent. Finally, even the most advanced system can only recognize threats whose signals it can observe: if those signals are not collected or interpreted correctly, the attack may go unnoticed.

The challenges of defense become even more apparent when cyberattacks have consequences in the physical world. Cyber tools have also become genuine offensive weapons in contemporary conflicts. Missiles and explosives are not necessarily needed to strike essential services: compromising power grids, hospitals, transportation, communications, or food distribution systems can cause disruption and economic losses and, in the most serious cases, put people’s lives at risk, indirectly or even directly. Of course, not every cyberattack is a military operation, but the digital domain is now an integral part of conflicts. And AI agent swarms, in some respects, resemble another technology that is changing how wars are fought: drones. Although they are very different tools, they share one important feature: they can multiply threats, putting defenders under pressure.

The war in Ukraine has shown how relatively inexpensive drones can be deployed in large numbers, forcing defenders to spend far more to intercept them. A sophisticated interceptor missile can cost many times more than the drone it is meant to shoot down, and when attacks multiply, the economic sustainability of defense becomes a problem in its own right. That is why Ukraine also uses surprisingly simple solutions, such as protective nets installed over roads to hinder drone attacks. According to Ukraine's Ministry of Defence, more than 2,200 kilometres of frontline roads had been equipped with anti-drone protection by November 2026. It is almost a paradox: in a war dominated by highly advanced technology, relatively simple physical barriers are proving useful again. The same lesson applies to cybersecurity: the best response to a sophisticated threat is not always an even more sophisticated technology. AI can help, but we also need updated systems, segmented networks, and, where possible, a decision not to connect devices to the Internet when they do not really need it.

This leads to another question: are we sure that a more digitized society is necessarily a safer one? Some countries have long recognized the importance of maintaining alternatives to digital services. In Sweden and the Netherlands, for example, authorities explicitly recommend keeping cash available in case electronic payments are disrupted. The Swedish central bank suggests around SEK 1,000 per adult, while the Dutch central bank recommends approximately €70 per adult to prepare for a possible 72-hour disruption. In a very different context, during its June 2025 conflict with Israel, Iran severely restricted Internet access, with authorities citing concerns about the alleged misuse of communication networks for military purposes. The restrictions, which culminated in a near-total shutdown, also severely disrupted ordinary citizens' communications. These are very different situations, but they help illustrate an often-overlooked point: depending entirely on digital, interconnected technologies can, in certain circumstances, become a weakness. This does not mean going back to the past or giving up innovation, but preventing a malfunction or cyberattack from paralyzing essential services.

The issue goes far beyond protecting individual systems. Electronic payments, food distribution, transportation, energy, and communications are now closely interconnected. As the supermarket incidents show, even a limited attack can have tangible consequences for everyday life. But what would happen if a disruption affected several essential services and lasted for days? As early as 2025, the European Union adopted a strategy calling for guidelines to help citizens remain self-sufficient for at least 72 hours in an emergency. In the United Kingdom, people are advised to keep supplies of water, food, cash, and even battery-powered radios, useful when the Internet and other services are unavailable. These are general precautions intended for blackouts, natural disasters, and other emergencies as well, not just cyberattacks.

At first glance, these recommendations might seem overly cautious. But when I still read about default passwords that have never been changed, services accessible directly from the Internet without adequate protection, and machines that work perfectly well but run software their manufacturers have stopped updating, I grow concerned. The old IT mantra, “If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it”, is becoming dangerous: a system can continue to work flawlessly while remaining vulnerable to attack. And my concern grows when I think about the complexity of IT infrastructures, built up over time by layering software developed by different people and companies, often using different technologies, and connecting an ever-growing number of services. Add to that cameras, sensors, and other devices sometimes purchased without sufficient checks on their security. And as we continue to make everything more connected, we are developing AI systems increasingly capable of finding and exploiting precisely these weaknesses.

All the ingredients for a perfect mess are there. Let's hope for the best.

When Threats Move at Machine Speed, Governments Still Think at Human Speed

#9733. CertiK and Columbia University Bring Math Proofs to the GPU Code Behind Every Large AI Model

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta plan to spend about $725 billion on capital projects in 2026, most of it on AI data centers and chips, while the cost of the largest AI training runs has grown about 2.4 times a year since 2016 and is on track to pass $1 billion by 2027. Nearly all of that money turns into time on graphics processing units (GPUs). Every second of that time runs through kernels, the small, heavily tuned programs that tell a GPU how to multiply large tables of numbers or how to compute attention, the step that lets a language model weigh every word against every other word.

Those kernels are some of the most valuable code in AI and some of the hardest to check. A bug in one rarely crashes anything, so the job keeps running while quietly producing wrong numbers that flow into the next step of training or into the answers a model gives. CertiK and researchers at Columbia University have now built TensorLean, a system that uses mathematics to prove a production GPU kernel computes what it should. The team has applied it to more than 100 kernels from DeepSeek and the widely used FlashAttention library, finding 25 bugs along the way.

The 2026 plans are large at every company. Amazon expects to approach $200 billion, Microsoft has guided to $190 billion for the calendar year, Alphabet to between $180 billion and $190 billion and Meta to between $125 billion and $145 billion, while Alphabet has already told investors that its spending will rise significantly again in 2027. Hardware such as chips, servers and the networking between them makes up 47% to 67% of the cost of developing a frontier model, so the efficiency of that hardware is where most of the money is won or lost.

That efficiency is decided by kernels. FlashAttention, the open-source attention library with more than 25,000 stars on GitHub, supplies features used in models such as Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 and Grok, while DeepSeek released kernels such as DeepGEMM, which reaches up to 1,550 trillion operations a second on an H800 GPU. Because a training cluster runs the same few kernels billions of times, a small speed gain in one of them is worth more than almost any other software change, which is why some of the best engineers in AI spend their careers making kernels faster.

The TensorLean team puts the stakes in simple terms. If a training run spends $100 million on compute and 1% of that work must be repeated because of an error, the extra cost is $1 million. At the $1 billion scale Epoch AI expects the largest runs to reach by 2027, the same 1% would cost $10 million (our arithmetic). Failures are already routine at that scale: Meta's Llama 3 405B run on 16,384 H100 GPUs saw 419 unexpected interruptions over 54 days, about one every 3.1 hours.

The failures that crash a job are the easy ones, since the job stops and restarts from a saved checkpoint. The hard ones are silent: Meta traced six interruptions in a 54-day window to silent data corruption, where a chip returns a wrong answer without any error, while Google has estimated one such event every one to two weeks during Gemini training. Researchers at Harvard and Amazon found that a model's loss curve, the main health signal engineers watch, can look normal while its weights drift away from where they should be. A bug in a kernel behaves like silent corruption with one difference that makes it costlier, because a faulty chip affects one machine while a faulty kernel is copied to every GPU that runs it.

FlashAttention shows how quickly the code has changed. The second version ran at about 350 trillion operations a second on Nvidia's H100, around 35% of the chip's peak, before FlashAttention-3 reached 740 trillion in July 2024, about 75% of peak, with close to 1.2 quadrillion using 8-bit numbers. FlashAttention-4 then reached 1,613 trillion operations a second on Nvidia's newer B200 in March 2026, a 4.6-fold rise in under three years across two chip generations.

Each jump came from a trick that makes the code harder to reason about. The kernels copy data while doing math at the same time, assign some groups of GPU threads only to loading data while others only compute, change how they split the work depending on the size of the input and use lower-precision numbers such as FP8, which doubles speed but adds rounding. Testing checks a kernel on the inputs someone thought to try, so a bug that only appears for one unusual input size, or only when a copy finishes a moment late, can pass every test and still ship.

Formal verification replaces examples with proof. A tester runs a program on chosen inputs and checks the outputs, while a formal proof shows mathematically that the program meets its requirements for every input inside a defined range. TensorLean writes these proofs in Lean, a proof language in which a small, trusted checker confirms every step, so anyone can rerun the check and get the same answer without trusting the people who wrote the proof.

The system works on PTX, the low-level instruction set Nvidia's compiler produces just before code runs on a GPU, so the proof covers the code that actually executes after the compiler has made its changes. TensorLean models the speed tricks together, including data transfers that overlap with computation, layouts that change with the size of the task and lower-precision arithmetic held to set numerical tolerances.

Specifications written for one kernel can be reused for related kernels, which lets the approach spread to more code and repeat each time that code changes. That reuse is what makes the method practical for teams that ship new optimizations every few weeks.

The team has applied TensorLean to more than 100 production GPU kernels across several generations of GPU architecture, including kernels from DeepSeek and from FlashAttention. The work uncovered two bugs in DeepSeek's kernels and 23 in FlashAttention. When a proof fails, it points to the case that breaks. Once the code is repaired, the team proves the new version again so the fix is confirmed to meet its requirements.

The choice of targets matters because both codebases are shared. FlashAttention has more than 3,000 forks on GitHub while DeepSeek's kernels were released openly for anyone to build on, which means a bug in either one travels into many other projects. A fix proved at the source protects every team downstream, which turns one research effort into a gain for a large part of the open-source AI stack.

For teams that train or serve large models, TensorLean fits into the work they already do. After each round of optimization an engineer can measure the speed gain, rerun verification to check that the change did not introduce a computational error and, when the code meets its requirements, keep a machine-checkable proof alongside it. That record lowers the risk of wasted compute, costly training reruns and wrong results feeding into later calculations, which are the losses that grow with every increase in cluster size.

The need will grow as AI writes more of its own code. Researchers are already using language-model agents to generate GPU kernels and prove them correct in Lean. Kernel code produced that way will arrive faster than any human team can review it. The practical starting point is the code that runs most often, such as attention, matrix multiplication and mixture-of-experts routing, where a proof protects the largest share of compute and where specifications can be reused across versions.

Formal verification has a long history in systems software. seL4 became the first fully verified operating system kernel in 2009. CertiKOS, a verified concurrent operating system kernel, followed at Yale with Ronghui Gu as a lead designer. Gu and Yale professor Zhong Shao founded CertiK in 2017. The company has since worked with more than 5,500 enterprise and institutional clients and found more than 119,000 code vulnerabilities.

AI has made proofs far cheaper to produce. DeepMind's AlphaProof reached silver-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad in 2024 with proofs written in Lean, while Anthropic formalized Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean with Claude in 11 days in September, producing about 13 million lines. In October, Claude worked with the firm Theorem to prove 123 open-source libraries free of crashes with about 180 million lines of proof, roughly 900 times the size of the seL4 proof (our arithmetic). TensorLean carries that progress into the computing code that AI itself runs on.

As training budgets head toward $1 billion per run, a proof of correctness is likely to become as routine a part of shipping a kernel as a speed benchmark is today. Teams that can prove each optimization correct can push for speed with more confidence, while teams that rely on testing alone carry a growing risk of finding errors only after the compute has been spent.

For CertiK, TensorLean extends formal verification from blockchains and operating systems into AI infrastructure, the fastest-growing category of computing spend. The next test is adoption: whether the labs and library maintainers who write the fastest kernels start shipping proofs alongside them, which would give the industry a firmer base for every gain in AI computing efficiency that follows.

#9732. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

Find puerquitos and many more Mexican sweets in our feature celebrating pan dulce.

#9729. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier



 In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

So let’s dive into

1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Pros:

  • Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts
  • Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion
  • Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing
  • Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt.

Cons:

  • May generate text that is biased or offensive
  • Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct
  • May require large amounts of computational resources to run
  • The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

  • May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data
  • May require significant computational resources to run
  • The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

3. Lumen5

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Pros:

  • Automatically summarizes text from a blog post, article, or another source into a script for a video or social media post
  • Offers a library of royalty-free videos, images, and music to use in content
  • Has a drag-and-drop interface for easy content creation
  • Can create videos in multiple languages
  • Has a built-in analytics tool to track the performance of created content.

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material
  • The automatic summarization feature may not always capture the main points of the source material
  • The library of videos, images, and music is limited.
  • The analytics feature is basic

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

4. Grammarly

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

Pros:

  • Checks for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text
  • Provides suggestions for improving clarity, concision, and readability
  • Can be integrated with various apps and platforms such as Microsoft Office, Google Docs, and social media platforms
  • Offers a browser extension and a desktop app
  • Has a premium version with more advanced features such as plagiarism detection and more

Cons:

  • The suggestions provided may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The grammar checker may not always recognize context-specific language use
  • The free version has limited features
  • Limited to English language only
  • Overall, Grammarly is a useful tool for improving writing, it can help users identify and correct grammar and punctuation errors, and improve the clarity, concision, and readability of their text. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate.

5.OpenAI Codex

OpenAI Codex is a system developed by OpenAI that can create code from natural language descriptions of software tasks. The system is based on the GPT-3 model and can generate code in multiple programming languages.

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of writing code
  • Can help developers to be more productive
  • Can help non-technical people to create software
  • Can generate code in multiple programming languages

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description
  • The generated code may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex software tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, OpenAI Codex is a powerful tool that can help automate the process of writing code and make it more accessible to non-technical people. However, the quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description and it is important to review and test the code before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

6. Tabnine

Tabnine is a code completion tool that uses AI to predict and suggest code snippets. It is compatible with multiple programming languages and can be integrated with various code editors.

Pros:

  • Can improve coding efficiency by suggesting code snippets based on context
  • Can complete entire code blocks
  • Can predict variables, functions, and other elements of code
  • Can be integrated with various code editors

Cons:

  • The suggestions may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The system may not always be able to understand the context of the code
  • May not work with all code editors
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, TabNine is a useful tool for developers that can help improve coding efficiency and reduce the time spent on writing code. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

7. Jasper AI

Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Pros:

  • User-friendly interface
  • Generates a wide variety of content types
  • Guarantees 100% unique and free-plagiarism content
  • SEO friendly
  •  Create articles of up to 10k words

Cons:

  • Not the cheapest AI writer on the market

8. Surfer SEO

Surfer SEO is a software tool designed to help website owners and digital marketers improve their search engine optimization (SEO) efforts. The tool provides a variety of features that can be used to analyze a website's on-page SEO, including:

Features:

  • A site audit tool that checks for technical SEO issues
  • A content editor that suggests optimizations for individual pages
  • A keyword research tool that suggests keywords to target
  • A SERP analyzer that shows how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • A backlink analysis tool that shows the backlinks pointing to a website.

Pros:

  • Can help website owners and marketers identify technical SEO issues
  • Can provide suggestions for optimizing individual pages
  • Can help with keyword research
  • Can show how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • Can provide insight into a website's backlink profile

Cons:

  • Some features may require a paid subscription
  • The tool is not a guarantee of better ranking
  • The tool can only analyze the data it has access to
  • The tool's suggestions may not always be applicable or optimal

Overall, Surfer SEO can be a useful tool for website owners and digital marketers looking to improve their SEO efforts. However, it is important to remember that it is just a tool and should be used in conjunction with other SEO best practices. Additionally, the tool is not a guarantee of better ranking.

9. Zapier

Zapier is a web automation tool that allows users to automate repetitive tasks by connecting different web applications together. It does this by creating "Zaps" that automatically move data between apps, and can also be used to trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Features:

  • Can connect over 3,000 web applications
  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can create "Zaps" to move data between apps
  • Can trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Pros:

  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can save time
  • Can improve workflow
  • Can increase productivity
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of web applications

Cons:

  • Can be difficult to set up
  • May require some technical skills
  • May require a paid subscription for some features
  • Some apps may not be compatible
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the apps

Overall, Zapier is a useful tool that can help users automate repetitive tasks and improve workflow. It can save time and increase productivity by connecting different web applications together. However, it may require some technical skills and some features may require a paid subscription. It is important to use the tool with caution and not to rely too much on it, to understand the apps better.

10. Compose AI

Compose AI is a company that specializes in developing natural language generation (NLG) software. Their software uses AI to automatically generate written or spoken text from structured data, such as spreadsheets, databases, or APIs.

Features:

  • Automatically generates written or spoken text from structured data
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources
  • Can be used for a variety of applications such as creating reports, summaries, and explanations
  • Provides an API and a user-friendly interface

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of creating written or spoken content
  • Can help users create more accurate and consistent content
  • Can help users save time by automating repetitive tasks
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source
  • The generated content may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the data

Overall, Compose AI's NLG software can be a useful tool for automating the process of creating written or spoken content from structured data. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source, and it is essential to review the generated content before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the understanding of the data.

Conclusion

AI tools are becoming increasingly important in today's business and technology landscape. They are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The top 10 AI tools included in this article are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for various applications. Whether you're looking to improve your natural language processing, create high-resolution images, or optimize your website, there is an AI tool that can help. It's important to research and evaluate the different tools available to determine which one is the best fit for your specific needs. As AI technology continues to evolve, these tools will become even more powerful and versatile and will play an even greater role in shaping the future of business and technology.

#9721. 16 pumpkin recipes, from cakes and cookies to bars and bread: We've got a marbled pumpkin cake, chewy pumpkin cookies, and even pumpkin milk bread.

It’s that time of year when pumpkin spice everything starts appearing on store shelves — candles, lip balm, air fresheners, beer, and of course, the ubiquitous PSL (pumpkin spice latte). That means fall is here, and more importantly, that pumpkin should make a grand return to your kitchen! Pull out your canned pumpkin — or better yet, make your own pumpkin purée — and stock your pantry with pumpkin pie spice, because we have the best pumpkin recipes to bake this fall.

This Pumpkin Swirl Cake takes my breath away every time I unmold it from its intricate loaf pan. The anticipation keeps building until I slice into the pound cake-like loaf and reveal the swirled pattern inside, marbled with both vanilla and spiced pumpkin batter. (Don’t fret if you don’t have the specialty loaf pan — this can also be baked in a standard loaf pan and adorned with a simple confectioners’ sugar icing.)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Patch O Pumpkins Loaf Pan and Pure Vanilla Plus

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Sparkling Sugar

A cousin of Belgian-style Liège waffles, these Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles have caramelized edges and a pleasant chew that’s reminiscent of brioche. The yeasted batter has pumpkin in it for flavor and color, plus Swedish pearl sugar that melts into pockets of crispy sugar. The best part? The batter rests overnight, so if you prepare it the night ahead, all you have to do the next morning is scoop and cook the batter for hot, crispy waffles in just a few minutes.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles

To make this recipe, you'll need: Swedish Pearl Sugar

I used to make the same pumpkin pie recipe for years, and it always left me wanting a little more excitement. Then I found this Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie and never looked back! The generously spiced filling uses nutmeg, ginger, cloves, and Vietnamese cinnamon to create a more flavorful pie than traditional versions. The secret to its silky-smooth texture? Corn syrup, which is an invert sugar and keeps the custard from becoming grainy. Substitute another invert sugar like honey or maple syrup if you like; I use maple syrup.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

Whenever I have these tender, golden scones on hand, I look forward to getting out of bed the next morning because I know they’re waiting for me. They can be easily customized to use a range of mix-ins, depending on what you have in your pantry. My personal preference is a mix of crystallized ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits.

Get the recipe: Harvest Pumpkin Scones (or Gluten-Free Pumpkin Scones)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Mini Diced Ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits

If you’re looking for a way to make your whole kitchen smell like fall, these one-bowl, easy pumpkin muffins deliver — and fast. They’re ready in under an hour, so you can spend less time measuring, mixing, and cleaning and more time tackling your autumn bucket list.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Standard Muffin Pan

Making banana bread is an almost weekly activity in my house — except during fall, when we pivot to pumpkin bread instead. This is a quick, easy bake that satisfies my craving for something pumpkin-y, and it uses a simple trick to concentrate the pumpkin flavor and ensure the loaf is perfectly textured: The pumpkin purée is reduced on the stovetop to cook off excess moisture. (The process is similar to browning butter.) As a result, the final loaf is packed with pumpkin flavor.

Get the recipe: The Most Pumpkin Pumpkin Chocolate Chip Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: Ginger and Semisweet Chocolate Chips

These bars have all the cozy, spiced goodness of the classic dessert in a portable, crowd-friendly form. The buttery, brown sugar crust gets pressed into the pan (no rolling out pie dough!), and the silky pumpkin filling comes together with just a handful of ingredients. The (optional but highly recommended) sour cream whipped topping brings a slight tanginess and completes the traditional pumpkin pie experience.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Milk Bread is exceptionally soft, squishy, and feather-light, while also packing in a lot of pumpkin. Pumpkin can often weigh down baked goods, but here the combination of a tangzhong, bread flour, and a long mix makes this bread simultaneously moist and high-rising.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Yeast

This tender pumpkin crumb cake is for people who double the chocolate chips in pumpkin bread and the streusel on coffee cake. Atop the thin layer of spiced pumpkin cake lays a heavy blanket of buttery crumbs with a bold chocolate flavor, thanks to Dutch-processed cocoa powder.

Get the recipe: Chocolate-Pumpkin Crumb Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Black Cocoa

These Pumpkin Cupcakes, with their piped swirl of cream cheese frosting, are the ideal way to celebrate fall birthdays. The cupcakes are super tender, thanks to the addition of cake flour and oil. Sour cream and brown sugar add tanginess and molasses-y sweetness while also preventing the cupcakes from being dry.

For more cupcake decorating ideas, see our YouTube video: Decorate Cupcakes Better Than Ever.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cake Flour (or Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour)

My husband’s favorite fall dessert is Pumpkin Whoopie Pies, hands down. He can’t resist these subtly sweet cakes sandwiching rich cream cheese filling. This recipe has a few extra bells and whistles to take it over the top: Bread and Cake Enhancer to keep the cakes extra soft and fresh, xanthan gum in the filling to give it a smooth mouthfeel, and diced crystallized ginger for a bit of extra zing in the filling.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Bread and Cake Enhancer, Xanthan Gum, and Mini Diced Ginger

The next time there’s a rainy weekend, I’m taking on a project bake: our Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish. It’s a multiday process and laminating dough is a labor of love, but the final product is worth the effort: buttery, crisp pastries filled with pumpkin and sweet cream cheese.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting is a show-stopping dessert featuring spiced layers of cake, not-too-sweet cream cheese frosting, and a blanket of melted caramel poured over the top. Will it be slightly messy to serve? Yes. Will anyone mind? Absolutely not.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Offset Spatula

The pumpkin spice recipe I’m most excited to bake this fall is a mash-up of greats: Part-coffee cake, part-Bundt cake, part-pumpkin bread, this Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake deserves a category all of its own. It has two layers of espresso swirl tucked within a moist, spiced cake. Make it in your favorite Bundt pan or serve it as a loaf if you’re more of simple-is-better person. Either way, it’s great for snacking all day long.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Espresso Powder and Bundt Pan

#9716. WiCi Infer Runs 800B-Parameter AI Models on a Laptop by Streaming Them From the SSD

Communications Strategist & Technology Builder 🔮 Partner Zen Media | Building the human layer between brands and AI

Communications Strategist & Technology Builder 🔮 Partner Zen Media | Building the human layer between brands and AI

Communications Strategist & Technology Builder 🔮 Partner Zen Media | Building the human layer between brands and AI

WiCi, the systems research lab behind the WiCi One wireless GPU, has released WiCi Infer, a free desktop app built to run large local LLMs on a personal computer. It runs 800B-parameter models on Macs and Windows PCs that can hold only a fraction of the model in memory. Until now, running a model that size has meant owning more memory than any laptop ships with.

The app does not load the full model into RAM or GPU memory before it answers. It keeps the weights on the computer's SSD and pulls in the parts each step needs.

WiCi Infer is built on InferSSD, the open-source inference engine the company recently released. Both make the same argument: frontier AI should run on hardware people already own, without a data center behind it.

WiCi Infer stores the model on the SSD and moves only the active portion into memory as text is generated. That works because the models it targets are mixture-of-experts designs, which route each token through a small subset of their weights. Muse Spark Open has 816 billion parameters, and about 42 billion are active at a time, according to WiCi.

InferSSD, which is built on llama.cpp, keeps those routed expert weights on disk. The shared layers, attention and working cache still have to fit in RAM or GPU memory, as WiCi explains in its write-up on running 800B-parameter LLMs on consumer hardware. Memory requirements shrink. They do not disappear.

That changes the hardware math for local AI. The files for an 800B-class model take up about 520GB, more than ten times the memory in a well-equipped laptop. With WiCi Infer, storage carries that load.

Diagram showing WiCi Infer keeping about 520GB of model weights on the SSD and streaming active expert weights into RAM or GPU memory to generate tokens

How WiCi Infer runs an 800B-parameter model: weights stay on the SSD and only the active experts move into memory.

WiCi's published benchmarks show about 2.7 tokens per second running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on an Apple M5 Max MacBook Pro with 48GB of memory. Standard llama.cpp reached about 0.9 tokens per second on the same machine in WiCi's tests, which puts InferSSD at roughly three times the speed.

The same laptop produces about one token per second with Muse Spark Open, against 0.15 for llama.cpp.

Those speeds are slow next to smaller models or cloud AI services. At 2.7 tokens per second, a 300-word answer takes about two and a half minutes. The news is that models of this size run on a laptop at all.

The figures are WiCi's own, not independent tests. Results will vary with the computer, the model and the settings.

Bar chart of WiCi's published benchmarks on a 48GB M5 Max MacBook Pro comparing InferSSD and llama.cpp tokens per second for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Muse Spark Open

Decode speed on a 48GB M5 Max MacBook Pro, in tokens per second. Source: WiCi published benchmarks.

Yes, according to the company. WiCi Infer serves the loaded model through a local OpenAI-compatible API, so existing coding, writing and document tools can connect to a model running on the same machine. WiCi says prompts are processed locally, not on a cloud AI service, and the app requires no account or login.

For teams working with sensitive documents, source code or private business data, that is a practical reason to run a model locally. It also puts the choice of model, and where data is processed, in the user's hands.

The app has a graphical interface for downloading, launching and managing models, so no command line is required. The InferSSD engine underneath is open source, which lets developers inspect and build on it.

WiCi also makes WiCi One, a wireless GPU for local AI workloads. WiCi Infer applies the same idea in software: get more out of the hardware a person already has.

Large models have outgrown personal computers. Memory requirements climbed past what a desktop or laptop offers, which left cloud services as the practical option for most people.

WiCi Infer offers a second option by leaning on storage. The trade-off is plain: users need about 520GB of free SSD space, and generation is slow compared with the cloud. In return, an 800B-class model runs on a personal computer, privately, at no cost for the software.

#9707. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.
